modules.title: Market basics
modules.subtitle: What you actually buy, and how prices move

cards.title: A small piece of a company
cards.body: A stock (share) is a unit of ownership in a company. If a company has 1,000,000 shares and you own 100, you own 0.01% of it – of its profits, its assets and its future.

cards.title: Why companies sell shares
cards.body: Selling shares lets a company raise money without taking a loan: to build factories, hire people or develop products. In return, shareholders share in the company's future – good or bad.

cards.question: You own 500 of a company's 50,000 shares. What do you own?
cards.explain: 500 / 50,000 = 1%. A share is ownership, not a loan.

cards.title: What ownership gives you
cards.body: Shareholders may receive part of the profits (dividends), usually get a vote at the annual meeting, and benefit if the company grows. Small holders have a small voice – but the same rights per share.

cards.title: Owners are paid last
cards.body: If a company goes bankrupt, its lenders, suppliers and employees are paid first. Shareholders get what is left – often nothing. That is why a stock can fall to zero, and why owning one is riskier than lending.

cards.question: A company goes bankrupt. Who is usually paid first?
cards.explain: Lenders come before owners. Shareholders carry the most risk.

cards.title: Price is an agreement, not a fact
cards.body: A share price is simply the last price a buyer and a seller agreed on. It reflects what people expect about the company's future – and those expectations change every second.

cards.title: Tickers
cards.body: Every listed stock has a short code called a ticker – for example AAPL for Apple on Nasdaq. Brokers, charts and news all use it. Check the ticker carefully: similar names can belong to very different companies.

cards.question: What is a ticker?
cards.explain: A ticker identifies the stock, e.g. AAPL.

cards.title: Private vs. public
cards.body: Most companies are private: their shares belong to founders and investors and cannot be bought on an exchange. A public company has listed its shares so anyone can trade them.

cards.title: The IPO
cards.body: An Initial Public Offering is the first sale of shares to the public. Banks help set a price, the shares are sold, and from the next day they trade on the exchange.

cards.title: Primary and secondary market
cards.body: In the IPO (the primary market) the company receives the money. Afterwards, investors trade with each other (the secondary market) – the company gets nothing from those trades.

cards.question: You buy a share from another investor on the exchange. Who gets your money?
cards.explain: That's the secondary market: investors trade with each other.

cards.title: Why the hype is risky
cards.body: IPOs get headlines, and first-day jumps are famous. But a new stock has little trading history, insiders may sell once their lock-up period ends, and later results vary widely.

cards.title: What a public company must share
cards.body: Listed companies must publish regular financial reports and important news. In Israel these appear on the Magna system; in the US on the SEC's EDGAR. Original filings beat rumors.

cards.question: In an IPO, the money from the new shares goes to…
cards.explain: The IPO is the primary market – the company raises money.

cards.question: Which is true about IPO stocks?
options: They always rise in year one
They can't fall below the IPO price
cards.explain: New listings are hard to judge – there is little history to study.

cards.title: The exchange
cards.body: An exchange (like the NYSE, Nasdaq or the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange) is a regulated marketplace where buyers' and sellers' orders meet and are matched by computer.

cards.title: The broker
cards.body: You don't trade on the exchange directly. A licensed broker – an online trading platform or your bank – sends your orders, holds your shares for you, and charges fees for it.

cards.question: How does a private person reach the exchange?
cards.explain: Brokers connect you to the exchange and hold your assets.

cards.title: Regular hours
cards.body: US exchanges trade 9:30–16:00 New York time – usually 16:30–23:00 in Israel. Since January 2026 the Tel Aviv exchange trades Monday to Friday, with a shorter Friday.

cards.title: Before and after hours
cards.body: Some brokers allow pre-market and after-hours trading. Fewer people trade then, so spreads are wider and prices jump more. Crypto is different: it trades 24/7, including weekends.

cards.question: Why is after-hours trading riskier?
options: Fewer traders: wider spreads, bigger jumps
cards.explain: Less activity means less liquidity.

cards.title: The opening bell
cards.body: Overnight news piles up, so the first minutes after the open are often the most volatile of the day. Many experienced traders watch the open before acting.

cards.title: Your money at a broker
cards.body: Choose a broker licensed by a real regulator. Licensed brokers must keep client money separate from their own. An offshore 'broker' with no license offers no such protection.

cards.question: What should you check first about a broker?
options: That a real regulator licenses it
cards.explain: A license (and segregated client money) matters most.

cards.title: Supply and demand
cards.body: A price moves when buyers and sellers disagree. More eager buyers than sellers pushes the price up; more eager sellers pushes it down.

cards.title: Eagerness, not numbers
cards.body: Every trade has exactly one buyer and one seller, so 'more buyers than sellers' really means buyers are more eager: they accept higher prices to get filled.

cards.question: Buyers are more eager than sellers. The price usually…
cards.explain: Eager buyers lift their bids until sellers agree.

cards.title: Bid and ask
cards.body: The bid is the highest price someone will pay right now. The ask is the lowest price someone will sell for. A trade happens when they meet.

cards.title: The spread
cards.body: The gap between bid and ask is the spread. It is a hidden cost: if you buy at the ask and sell immediately at the bid, you lose the spread.

cards.question: Bid is 99.90 and ask is 100.10. What is the spread?

cards.title: Spreads differ
cards.body: A giant stock traded by millions may have a spread of one cent. A small, rarely traded stock or coin can have a spread of several percent – a cost you pay on every round trip.

cards.question: You want to buy right now. Which price do you pay?
cards.explain: Buying immediately takes the best seller's price: the ask.

cards.question: Which usually has the widest spread?
cards.explain: Thin trading means wide spreads.

cards.title: The order book
cards.body: The order book lists the waiting orders: buyers' bids on one side, sellers' asks on the other, each with a price and a size. The best bid and best ask sit at the top.

cards.title: Depth
cards.body: Depth is how much size waits near the current price. A deep book can absorb a large order with a small price change. A thin book moves a lot when someone trades.

cards.question: What does the order book show?
cards.explain: Bids and asks waiting to be matched.

cards.title: Liquidity
cards.body: Liquidity is how easily you can buy or sell without moving the price. Liquid markets have tight spreads and deep books. Illiquid ones can trap you: you may not get out at a fair price.

cards.title: Volume
cards.body: Volume counts how many shares changed hands in a period. High volume means many participants and usually good liquidity. A price move on high volume is taken more seriously than one on low volume.

cards.question: A stock trades only a few hundred shares a day. You should expect…
cards.explain: Low volume = low liquidity.

cards.title: Walking the book
cards.body: If you buy more than the best ask offers, your order eats through the next asks at higher prices. Your average price ends up worse than the price you saw.

cards.question: A breakout happens on very low volume. It is…
cards.explain: Few participants = weak confirmation.

cards.title: Market order
cards.body: Buys or sells immediately at the best available price. Fast, but the final price can differ from what you saw, especially in fast markets.

cards.title: Limit order
cards.body: Sets the worst price you accept: a buy limit at 50 fills only at 50 or lower. You control the price, but it may never fill.

cards.question: You want to buy, but never above 40. Which order?
cards.explain: A limit caps the price you pay.

cards.title: Limit orders wait in the book
cards.body: A buy limit below the current price joins the order book and waits. It fills only if sellers come down to your price. A sell limit above the price waits for buyers to come up.

cards.title: Stop order
cards.body: Becomes a market order once price touches a level. Traders use a stop-loss to exit automatically if the trade goes wrong.

cards.question: What is a stop-loss for?
options: Exiting automatically when a trade goes wrong
cards.explain: It limits the loss. It cannot guarantee the exact exit price in a gap.

cards.title: Take-profit
cards.body: A take-profit is a sell limit placed above your entry: it closes the trade at your target. Together, a stop-loss and a take-profit define the trade before you enter it.

cards.question: Speed matters more than price. Which order?
cards.explain: A market order fills now, at whatever the book offers.

cards.question: You bought at 100. Where does a protective stop-loss go?
cards.explain: For a long trade the stop sits below the entry.

cards.title: Slippage
cards.body: Slippage is the difference between the price you expected and the price you got. It is small in liquid markets and large in thin or fast ones, and it usually works against you.

cards.title: Gaps
cards.body: A gap is when price opens far from the previous close, skipping the prices in between – often after earnings or overnight news. A stop at 95 can be filled at 88 if the stock opens at 88.

cards.question: Your stop is at 95. The stock closes at 97 and opens at 90. You are likely filled near…
cards.explain: The stop triggers at the open – the first available price.

cards.title: Stop-limit
cards.body: A stop-limit turns into a limit order, not a market order, when triggered. It avoids a terrible fill – but in a fast drop it may not fill at all, leaving you in a falling trade.

cards.question: What is the main risk of a stop-limit?
options: It may not fill in a fast move
It always fills at a worse price
cards.explain: Protection against bad prices, at the cost of maybe not exiting.

cards.title: Time in force
cards.body: A Day order expires at the close if it hasn't filled. A GTC order (Good 'Til Cancelled) stays until it fills or you cancel it – check your open orders so old ones don't surprise you.

cards.question: You placed a GTC buy limit last month and forgot it. What can happen?
cards.explain: GTC orders stay live until filled or cancelled.

cards.title: How to reduce slippage
cards.body: Trade liquid instruments, avoid the first minutes after big news, use limit orders when price matters, and keep your size small relative to the volume.

cards.question: Expected fill 50.00, actual fill 50.20 on a buy. The slippage is…
cards.explain: You paid 0.20 more than expected.

cards.title: Going long
cards.body: Going long means buying first and selling later. You profit if the price rises. Your maximum loss is what you paid – the price can't fall below zero.

cards.title: Going short
cards.body: Short selling is the reverse: you borrow shares from your broker, sell them now, and buy them back later to return them. You profit if the price falls.

cards.question: You are short at 50. The price falls to 40. You…
cards.explain: Sold at 50, buy back at 40: +10.

cards.title: The danger of shorts
cards.body: A price can rise without limit, so a short's possible loss is unlimited. Shorts also pay borrowing fees, and the broker can demand the shares back.

cards.title: Short squeeze
cards.body: When a heavily shorted stock rises, short sellers rush to buy back and cut their losses. Their buying pushes the price even higher – a short squeeze.

cards.question: What is the maximum possible loss on a short?
cards.explain: There is no ceiling on price, so there is no ceiling on the loss.

cards.title: Why beginners usually start long
cards.body: Long trades have a known maximum loss and no borrowing costs. Learn to manage risk on longs first. In this app's trading floor you trade long positions.

cards.question: A long position profits when…
cards.explain: Buy low, sell higher.

cards.question: A heavily shorted stock jumps on good news. Shorts rush to buy back. This is…
cards.explain: Forced buying feeds the rise.

cards.title: Market capitalization
cards.body: Market cap = share price × number of shares. A company with 10 million shares at $20 is worth $200 million on the market. It tells you size – the share price alone doesn't.

cards.question: Company A: $500 per share. Company B: $10 per share. Which is bigger?
options: Can't tell without the share count
cards.explain: Size = price × shares. A 'cheap' share can belong to a huge company.

cards.title: Large, mid, small
cards.body: Large caps (often over $10 billion) tend to be more stable and liquid. Small caps can grow faster but swing harder, and the smallest 'penny stocks' are favorite targets for manipulation.

cards.title: A low price isn't 'cheap'
cards.body: A $2 stock is not a bargain because it is $2. What matters is what you get for the whole company. Splitting one share into ten changes the price, not the value.

cards.question: A company splits each share into 2. Its market cap…
cards.explain: Twice the shares at half the price: same total.

cards.title: Sectors
cards.body: Companies are grouped into sectors: technology, healthcare, banks, energy, consumer goods and more. Stocks in the same sector often move together because the same news affects them.

cards.title: Hidden concentration
cards.body: Owning five chip makers feels like five bets, but it is close to one: a bad day for chips hits them all. Real diversification spreads money across different sectors.

cards.question: Your 5 stocks are all airlines. Oil prices jump. What is likely?
cards.explain: Same sector, same risk.

cards.title: An index
cards.body: An index tracks a basket of stocks, like the S&P 500 (500 large US companies) or the TA-35 (35 large Israeli companies). It shows how 'the market' is doing.

cards.title: Weighting
cards.body: Most big indices are weighted by market cap: larger companies count more. In the S&P 500 a handful of giants can move the whole index.

cards.question: What does the TA-35 track?
cards.explain: An index = a basket.

cards.title: An ETF
cards.body: An ETF is a fund that trades like a stock and usually copies an index. One purchase spreads your money across many companies.

cards.title: Fees matter
cards.body: Every fund charges a yearly management fee. Index funds are usually cheap, and over many years even a 1% difference in fees grows into a large amount.

cards.title: Why it matters
cards.body: Spreading money across many companies (diversification) reduces the damage any single company can do to you. It reduces risk – it does not remove it: the whole market can fall.

cards.question: What does an index ETF usually do?
cards.explain: It tracks the index's basket – no guarantees.

cards.question: The whole market falls 20%. A broad index ETF…
cards.explain: Diversification protects from single-company risk, not from market risk.

cards.title: What is a bond?
cards.body: A bond is a loan you give to a government or a company. It pays interest (the coupon) and returns your money at maturity – if the borrower can pay.

cards.title: Bond risk
cards.body: Bonds are usually calmer than stocks, but not risk-free. A weak company can default, and when interest rates rise, the prices of existing bonds fall.

cards.question: Interest rates rise. Prices of existing bonds usually…
cards.explain: New bonds pay more, so old ones must get cheaper to compete.

cards.title: Asset classes
cards.body: Money can go into stocks, bonds, cash deposits, commodities (gold, oil), currencies (forex) or crypto. Each behaves differently, and each has its own risks.

cards.title: Risk and return travel together
cards.body: Higher possible return comes with bigger swings and bigger possible losses. Anyone offering high returns with no risk is describing something that doesn't exist.

cards.question: Which pairing is correct?
options: Higher possible return – bigger possible loss
cards.explain: Risk and return travel together.

cards.title: Forex and commodities
cards.body: Currencies trade in pairs (EUR/USD, USD/ILS) and move on interest rates and economics. Commodities move on supply, weather and politics. Both are often traded with leverage – more on that later.

cards.question: Buying a government bond means…
cards.explain: A bond is a loan.

cards.title: Dividends
cards.body: A dividend is part of the profit paid out to shareholders, usually quarterly or yearly. Mature, profitable companies pay them more often than young, fast-growing ones.

cards.title: Not free money
cards.body: On the ex-dividend date, the share price usually drops by about the dividend amount. The value moved from the company to your pocket – and it may be taxed.

cards.question: A $100 stock pays a $2 dividend. On the ex-date the price is likely about…
cards.explain: The payout comes out of the company's value.

cards.title: Dividend yield
cards.body: Yield = yearly dividends ÷ share price. $4 a year on a $100 share is a 4% yield. A sudden very high yield is often a warning: the price fell because the dividend may be cut.

cards.question: $3 a year in dividends, share price $60. The yield is…

cards.title: Buybacks
cards.body: Instead of paying dividends, a company can buy its own shares back. Fewer shares remain, so each one represents a bigger slice of the profits.

cards.title: Total return
cards.body: Your real result is price change plus dividends received. A stock that went sideways for years but paid 4% a year still earned something; one that rose 10% and paid nothing earned 10%.

cards.question: A company buys back 10% of its shares. Each remaining share…
options: Owns a bigger slice of the company
cards.explain: Fewer shares share the same profits.

cards.title: Earnings season
cards.body: Public companies report results every quarter: revenue (sales), profit, and earnings per share (EPS). Many also give guidance – what they expect for the coming months.

cards.title: Expectations move prices
cards.body: Analysts publish forecasts before each report. The price reacts to the surprise, not the number itself: great results that were already expected can still send a stock down.

cards.question: Profit rose 30%, but analysts expected 40%. The stock may…
cards.explain: Markets trade the gap between results and expectations.

cards.title: Guidance often matters more
cards.body: A good quarter with weak guidance can disappoint, because prices look forward. Investors care most about future profits.

cards.title: Report days are gap days
cards.body: Reports usually come out before the open or after the close, so the stock often gaps the next session. Holding a trade through a report is a bet on the surprise – size it small or step aside.

cards.question: EPS stands for…
cards.explain: Profit divided by the number of shares.

cards.title: Read the source
cards.body: Headlines simplify and sometimes get it wrong. The company's own report and its official filing are the facts; everything else is someone's interpretation.

cards.question: Why are earnings days risky for a short-term trade?
options: The stock can gap past your stop
cards.explain: A gap can skip your stop level.

lessons.title: Interest rates, inflation and the market

cards.title: The central bank
cards.body: Central banks – the Federal Reserve in the US, the Bank of Israel here – set a key interest rate. It affects mortgages, loans, deposits and, indirectly, every asset price.

cards.title: Inflation
cards.body: Inflation is the general rise in prices, measured by the consumer price index (CPI). When inflation runs hot, central banks usually raise rates to cool it down.

cards.question: Inflation is high. What do central banks usually do?
cards.explain: Higher rates slow borrowing and spending.

cards.title: Why rates matter to stocks
cards.body: When safe deposits pay 5%, investors demand more from risky stocks, and companies pay more on their debt. Rising rates often pressure stock prices – especially fast-growing companies valued on distant profits.

cards.question: Rates rise sharply. Which stocks are often hit hardest?
options: Fast-growing companies valued on future profits
cards.explain: Distant profits are worth less when money today earns more.

cards.title: Scheduled market movers
cards.body: Rate decisions, inflation reports and jobs data are published on known dates. Markets can swing sharply in the minutes after – check the economic calendar before trading.

cards.title: No one forecasts this reliably
cards.body: Economists disagree, and markets often react the opposite way to what 'should' happen. Understand the forces; don't bet everything on one prediction.

cards.question: A rate decision is due in 10 minutes. A careful beginner…
options: Waits for the dust to settle
cards.explain: Big scheduled news = big, fast moves.

lessons.title: Bull markets, bear markets and volatility

cards.title: Bulls and bears
cards.body: A bull market is a long period of rising prices. A bear market is commonly defined as a fall of 20% or more from the peak. A drop of 10–20% is usually called a correction.

cards.question: An index falls 23% from its peak. This is usually called…
cards.explain: 20% or more from the peak.

cards.title: Both are normal
cards.body: Bear markets have happened again and again in history, and so have recoveries – but some recoveries took many years. Plans that only work when prices rise are not plans.

cards.title: Volatility
cards.body: Volatility is how much and how fast prices swing. A calm stock may move 1% a day; a small crypto coin can move 20%. Higher volatility means wider stops and smaller positions.

cards.question: A coin often moves 15% a day. Compared with a calm stock you should trade it with…
cards.explain: More swing per unit = fewer units for the same risk.

cards.title: The fear gauge
cards.body: The VIX index measures the volatility options traders expect in the S&P 500. It spikes in panics. High readings mean wild days, not a signal of direction.

cards.title: Emotions follow the market
cards.body: In bull markets people feel like geniuses and take bigger risks. In bear markets they panic and sell at the bottom. Knowing this pattern is the first step to not following it.

cards.question: The VIX jumps. This tells you…
cards.explain: It measures expected swings, not direction.

lessons.title: The real costs: fees and taxes

cards.title: Every trade costs something
cards.body: Commissions, the spread, currency conversion (shekels to dollars and back) and monthly account or custody fees all come out of your result – win or lose.

cards.question: You buy US stocks with shekels. Which cost might you forget?
cards.explain: Converting shekels to dollars (and back) costs money.

cards.title: Small costs, big effect
cards.body: Paying $5 each way on a $500 trade is 2% before the price moves at all. Frequent small trades can lose money even when your ideas are right.

cards.question: A $400 trade, $4 commission to buy and $4 to sell. Costs as a % of the trade:

cards.title: Taxes
cards.body: Profits are taxable. In Israel, an individual's real capital gains on securities are generally taxed at 25%, and losses can usually offset gains in the same year. Rules change – check with a tax advisor or your broker.

cards.title: Think in net
cards.body: A strategy that makes 10% a year before costs can make far less after commissions, spreads, conversion and tax. Always judge results net of every cost.

cards.question: A $1,000 account pays a $10 monthly account fee. Per year that is…
cards.explain: $120 a year on $1,000. Fixed fees hurt small accounts most.

cards.question: Which number tells you how you really did?
options: The result after all costs and tax
cards.explain: Only net results pay the bills.

cards.title: Gains and losses aren't symmetric
cards.body: Lose 50% and your $1,000 becomes $500. To get back to $1,000 you now need +100%. The deeper the hole, the harder the climb.

cards.question: After a 50% loss, what gain gets you back to even?

cards.title: The recovery table
cards.body: −10% needs +11%. −25% needs +33%. −50% needs +100%. −80% needs +400%. This is why protecting capital comes before chasing returns.

cards.question: A stock falls 25%. What rise brings it back?

cards.title: Compounding
cards.body: Compounding means earning returns on earlier returns. Small steady gains grow big over time: 7% a year roughly doubles money in about 10 years.

cards.title: Compounding exposes fake promises
cards.body: 'Just 1% a week' sounds modest, but compounded it is about +68% a year; '1% a day' would multiply money more than 30 times in a year. Claims like these are marketing, not math.

cards.question: Someone promises '1% a day, every day'. Over a year that would be…
cards.explain: 1.01^365 ≈ 37. No real strategy does that.

cards.question: Compounding works best with…
options: Steady returns and few big losses
cards.explain: Big losses break the compounding chain.

cards.title: What is leverage?
cards.body: Leverage lets you control a bigger position than your money. With 10× leverage, $1,000 controls $10,000 of an asset. The broker lends you the difference.

cards.title: It cuts both ways
cards.body: With 10× leverage a 5% move becomes 50% of your money. A 10% move against you wipes out your entire margin – even though the asset only fell 10%.

cards.question: 10× leverage, the asset falls 10%. Your margin…
cards.explain: 10% × 10 = 100% of your money.

cards.title: Margin call
cards.body: When losses eat into your margin, the broker asks for more money – a margin call. If you can't pay, it closes your position at the current price, often at the worst moment.

cards.question: What happens if you ignore a margin call?
cards.explain: Forced liquidation at market price.

cards.title: CFDs and leveraged products
cards.body: CFDs and similar products are built on leverage. European regulators require CFD providers to publish what share of their retail accounts lose money – it is typically a large majority.

cards.title: The beginner's rule
cards.body: Learn without leverage. Leverage doesn't make a strategy better – it only makes the results, and the mistakes, bigger and faster.

cards.question: What does leverage change?
options: The size of gains and losses
cards.explain: It magnifies outcomes – good and bad.

cards.title: Two time horizons
cards.body: Investors hold for years and care about the business. Traders hold for minutes to weeks and care about price movement.

cards.title: Trading styles
cards.body: Day traders close everything before the close. Swing traders hold for days to weeks. Position traders hold for weeks to months. Longer styles need less screen time and pay fewer costs.

cards.question: You hold trades for a few days to two weeks. Your style is…
cards.explain: Days to weeks = swing.

cards.title: The honest truth
cards.body: Short-term trading is hard. Costs, spreads and emotions work against you, and many beginners lose money. This app teaches skills – it does not promise profits.

cards.title: Only risk what you can lose
cards.body: Never trade with money you need for rent, bills or emergencies. Practice here first – the charts are simulated, so mistakes are free.

cards.question: Which statement is true?
options: Trading is a safe way to save
cards.explain: Losses are part of trading. Risk management is what keeps them small.

cards.title: Know which game you play
cards.body: Mixing styles causes damage: a 'trade' that goes wrong becomes a 'long-term investment' to avoid taking the loss. Decide the plan before entering, and stick to it.

cards.question: Your short-term trade hit its stop level. The disciplined move is…
cards.explain: Follow the plan you made with a clear head.

cards.title: A trading plan
cards.body: A plan answers five questions before any trade: what do I trade, why do I enter, where is my stop, how much do I risk, and when do I take profit?

cards.question: When should you decide where your stop goes?
cards.explain: Decisions made in advance are calmer.

cards.title: Rules you can follow
cards.body: Good rules are specific: 'I risk at most 1% per trade' beats 'I'll be careful'. If a rule can't be checked, it can't be followed.

cards.title: The journal
cards.body: Write down every trade: date, reason, entry, stop, target, exit, result – and how you felt. After 20–30 trades, patterns appear that memory hides.

cards.question: Why keep a trading journal?
options: To find patterns in your own mistakes
cards.explain: Memory is selective; a journal isn't.

cards.title: Practice before real money
cards.body: Paper trading – trading with virtual money – lets you test your plan without losses. Use the Chart Trainer and the trading floor in this app until your rules feel automatic.

cards.title: Judge the process, not one result
cards.body: A good trade can lose and a bad trade can win. Ask 'did I follow my plan?' rather than 'did I make money today?'. Over many trades, process drives results.

cards.question: You broke your rules and still made money. That trade was…
options: A bad trade with a lucky result
cards.explain: Luck isn't a repeatable process.

cards.question: Which is a usable rule?
options: Risk at most 1% of the account per trade
cards.explain: Specific and checkable.

exam.question: A share represents…
exam.explain: A share is a unit of ownership.

exam.question: In an IPO, the money for new shares goes to…
exam.explain: The IPO is the primary market.

exam.question: The ask is…
options: The lowest price a seller accepts
The highest price a buyer pays

exam.question: A thin, illiquid market usually means…
A buy limit at 50 fills at…
A short seller profits when…
exam.explain: Sell high now, buy back lower.

exam.question: Market capitalization is…
After a 50% loss you need… to get back to even
With 10× leverage, a 10% move against you…
Money for trading should be…
options: Money you can afford to lose

modules.title: Candlesticks
modules.subtitle: Read the story in every candle

cards.title: Four prices in one shape
cards.body: Each candle shows one period (a minute, an hour, a day): its Open, High, Low and Close – OHLC.

cards.title: Body and wicks
cards.body: The body spans open to close. The thin lines (wicks or shadows) reach the high and the low.

cards.question: What does the top of the upper wick show?
cards.explain: Wicks mark the extremes: high and low.

cards.title: Where they come from
cards.body: Candlestick charts were developed by Japanese rice traders centuries ago. Today they are the default on almost every trading platform because they pack a lot of information into a small space.

cards.title: Compared with a line chart
cards.body: A line chart connects only the closes. A candle also shows how far price traveled during the period and where it ended within that range – the battle, not just the result.

cards.question: A candle opened at 10, went up to 14, down to 9 and closed at 12. What is its high?
cards.explain: The high is the top of the upper wick: 14.

cards.title: Range
cards.body: The distance from the high to the low is the candle's range. Wide-range candles show strong activity; narrow ones show a quiet period.

cards.question: Same candle: open 10, close 12. How tall is the body?
cards.explain: Body = |close − open| = 2. The range (14 − 9) is 5.

cards.title: Every candle is a battle
cards.body: During each period, buyers try to push price up and sellers try to push it down. The candle's shape tells you who controlled the period and who won at the end.

cards.title: Where it closes matters most
cards.body: A close near the high means buyers were still in control at the end. A close near the low means sellers were. A close in the middle means neither side won.

cards.question: A candle closes right at its high. What does that suggest?
options: Buyers controlled the end of the period
cards.explain: Strong close = buyers were still pushing.

cards.title: Wicks are rejected prices
cards.body: A long upper wick means price went up but couldn't stay there: sellers pushed it back. A long lower wick means buyers rejected the low prices.

cards.question: A long upper wick shows that…
cards.explain: Price visited the high and was pushed back down.

cards.title: Big body, small body
cards.body: A big body shows conviction: one side moved price far and kept it there. A small body shows hesitation – the open and close ended up close together.

cards.title: Read, don't predict
cards.body: A single candle describes the past period. It doesn't tell you what comes next. Its value is in combining it with the trend and the location on the chart, as you'll learn.

cards.question: A big green body closing at the high shows…
cards.explain: It describes strength in the past period – not a promise.

cards.title: Green and red
cards.body: A bullish candle closes above its open (usually green). A bearish candle closes below its open (usually red).

cards.question: Open 20, close 23. The candle is…
cards.explain: Close above open = bullish.

cards.title: Reading a green candle
cards.body: In a green candle the open is at the bottom of the body and the close is at the top. In a red candle it's the opposite: open on top, close at the bottom.

cards.title: Colors are a setting
cards.body: Green-up/red-down is common, but some platforms use hollow and filled candles or other colors – and in parts of Asia red means up. Always check the legend.

cards.question: In a red (bearish) candle, where is the open?
options: At the top of the body
At the bottom of the body
At the tip of the lower wick
cards.explain: Bearish: opened high, closed lower.

cards.title: A green candle can still be weak
cards.body: If a green candle has a tiny body and a long upper wick, buyers lost most of their gains. Color says who won by a little; shape says how convincingly.

cards.title: Red can follow green
cards.body: A red candle can open higher than the previous close and still be red. Each candle compares only its own open and close.

cards.question: Green candle, tiny body, very long upper wick. Buyers…
cards.explain: The wick shows the rejected rally.

cards.title: One market, many pictures
cards.body: The same market looks different on a 5-minute chart and a daily chart. Patterns on longer timeframes are usually more meaningful.

cards.title: Candles nest inside each other
cards.body: One daily candle contains the whole day: on an hourly chart that's several candles. A clean hammer on the daily may look like a messy drop and bounce on the hourly.

cards.question: Patterns are usually more meaningful on…
cards.explain: More trading behind each candle.

cards.title: Noise on small timeframes
cards.body: 1-minute candles react to every single order. Many 'patterns' there are random noise, and costs eat a bigger share of small moves.

cards.title: Top-down reading
cards.body: A common habit: check the trend on a higher timeframe (daily), then look for timing on a lower one (hourly). Trading against the bigger trend is swimming against the current.

cards.question: The daily chart is in a clear downtrend. On the 5-minute chart you see a bullish candle. The bigger picture says…
options: The main trend is still down
cards.explain: One small candle doesn't change the daily trend.

cards.title: Pick your timeframe by your style
cards.body: Swing traders often use daily and 4-hour charts; day traders use 5- to 15-minute charts. Choose one main timeframe and stick to it while you learn.

cards.question: Why look at a higher timeframe first?
cards.explain: Context first, timing second.

cards.title: Marubozu: all body
cards.body: A marubozu has a big body and almost no wicks. A green one opened at the low and closed at the high: buyers controlled the entire period.

cards.question: A red marubozu means…
cards.explain: Opened at the high, closed at the low.

cards.title: Spinning top
cards.body: A spinning top has a small body in the middle and wicks on both sides. Both sides pushed, neither won. After a strong move it shows the momentum is slowing.

cards.title: Rejection wicks
cards.body: A wick at least twice the size of the body is a strong rejection of that price area. Rejections matter most at important levels, like a previous low or high.

cards.question: A candle has a body of 1 and a lower wick of 4. This shows…
cards.explain: The wick is 4× the body.

cards.title: Compare with the neighbors
cards.body: 'Big' and 'small' are relative. A candle twice the size of the last ten candles is big; the same candle in a wild market may be ordinary.

cards.question: After a long rally you see several spinning tops. They suggest…
cards.explain: Hesitation after strength – a warning, not a verdict.

cards.question: Is a candle with a 2-point body 'big'?
cards.explain: Size is relative to recent volatility.

cards.title: Three questions before any pattern
cards.body: What is the trend? Where on the chart is this happening? How big is it compared with recent candles? The same shape can mean opposite things in different places.

cards.title: Trend
cards.body: Reversal patterns need something to reverse. A 'bullish reversal' candle in the middle of a sideways range has no drop to reverse.

cards.question: A reversal pattern needs…
cards.explain: No trend, no reversal.

cards.title: Location
cards.body: Patterns at important levels – a previous low, a previous high, a round number – carry more weight than patterns in the middle of nowhere. You'll learn levels in module 4.

cards.title: Volume
cards.body: A reversal candle on unusually high volume shows many participants took part. The same shape on tiny volume is weaker evidence.

cards.question: Which hammer deserves more attention?
options: After a drop, at a previous low, high volume
In a flat range, low volume
cards.explain: Trend + location + volume = stronger evidence.

cards.title: Evidence, not certainty
cards.body: Think like a detective: each piece of context adds evidence. Even with all of it, the outcome is uncertain – that's why risk management comes with every setup.

cards.question: A perfect-looking pattern appears in a quiet sideways market. You should…
options: Trade it with a big size
Expect it to work for sure
cards.explain: Shape without context is weak.

cards.title: The shape
cards.body: After a drop, a candle with a small body and a long lower wick – at least twice the body.

cards.title: What it means
cards.body: Sellers pushed price down, but buyers brought it back near the open. It's a hint the drop is weakening – not a promise.

cards.title: The details
cards.body: Little or no upper wick, body in the top part of the range. The color of the body matters less, though a green hammer shows buyers finished slightly stronger.

cards.prompt: Find the Hammer on this chart

cards.question: Which candle is a Hammer?
options: Small body, long lower wick after a drop
cards.explain: A Hammer's lower wick is at least 2× its body.

cards.title: Where the stop usually goes
cards.body: Traders who act on a hammer often place the stop below the tip of its lower wick: if price breaks that low, the buyers' rejection has failed.

cards.question: A hammer's low is 48. A logical stop for a long trade sits…
options: At the open of the next candle
cards.explain: Below the low that buyers defended.

cards.prompt: Another one: tap the Hammer

cards.title: The Shooting Star
cards.body: After a rise, a small body with a long upper wick hints that buyers are tiring: they pushed higher, and sellers threw price back down.

cards.prompt: Find the Shooting Star

cards.question: A Shooting Star appears…
cards.explain: It warns that a rise may stall.

cards.title: Same shape, different place
cards.body: The shape of a hammer after a rise is called a Hanging Man – a warning for buyers. The shape of a shooting star after a drop is an Inverted Hammer – a weak hint of a bottom.

cards.question: A hammer-shaped candle appears after a long rise. It is called…
cards.explain: Name depends on the trend before it.

cards.title: Why the inverted hammer is weaker
cards.body: In an inverted hammer buyers tried to rally but failed to hold the high. It shows interest, not control, so traders usually wait for the next candle to confirm.

cards.question: Long upper wick, small body, after a drop. This is…
cards.explain: Shooting-star shape, but after a drop.

cards.question: Where would a trader acting on a shooting star place a protective stop for a short?
options: Above the top of the upper wick
cards.explain: If price breaks the rejected high, the idea failed.

cards.title: Open ≈ close
cards.body: A doji opens and closes at almost the same price. Buyers and sellers ended the period in balance.

cards.question: A doji mainly shows…
cards.explain: Balance between buyers and sellers.

cards.title: Dragonfly doji
cards.body: Open and close at the high, with a long lower wick: sellers drove price down and buyers erased it all. After a drop it resembles a hammer's message.

cards.title: Gravestone doji
cards.body: Open and close at the low, with a long upper wick: buyers pushed up and lost it all. After a rise it carries a similar warning to the shooting star.

cards.question: A doji with a long upper wick, open and close at the low, is…
cards.explain: Gravestone: the rally died and was buried.

cards.title: Context is everything
cards.body: A doji alone says 'undecided'. After a long trend it can warn of a pause; in a range it often means nothing. Often the best trade is no trade.

cards.prompt: Find the doji

cards.question: A lone doji in a quiet range. The best response is often…
cards.explain: No clear setup = no trade.

cards.title: Two candles
cards.body: A bullish engulfing: after a drop, a green body fully covers the previous red body. Bearish engulfing is the mirror after a rise.

cards.title: The story
cards.body: Day one: sellers in control. Day two: price opens at or below their close, then buyers take over and close above where day one opened. Control changed hands.

cards.question: In a bullish engulfing, the green body…
options: Fully covers the previous red body
Is smaller than the red body
cards.explain: It must engulf the prior body.

cards.title: Bodies, not wicks
cards.body: The classic definition compares bodies only. If the green body also engulfs the red candle's wicks, the signal is considered stronger.

cards.prompt: Spot the engulfing candle

cards.title: Patterns fail
cards.body: No pattern works every time. In the Chart Trainer about a third of patterns fail on Hard – just like real markets. That's why every trade needs a stop.

cards.question: Red body 50→47, then green body 46.5→51. Is it a bullish engulfing?
Where is the most logical stop for a bullish engulfing trade?
cards.explain: Below the low the buyers defended.

cards.title: The mirror image
cards.body: After a rise, a green candle is followed by a red one whose body fully covers it. Buyers were in control – then sellers took the whole day back and more.

cards.question: A bearish engulfing appears…
cards.explain: It warns the rise may end.

cards.prompt: Find the bearish engulfing

cards.title: What long holders do with it
cards.body: For someone already holding a long position, a bearish engulfing at a high is a reason to tighten the stop or take some profit – not necessarily to sell short.

cards.title: Size matters
cards.body: A big red candle that engulfs several previous candles shows a much stronger shift than one that barely covers a tiny green body.

cards.question: You hold a long position. A large bearish engulfing appears at the high. A reasonable response is…
options: Tighten the stop or take partial profit
cards.explain: Manage risk when the evidence changes.

cards.question: Do candle patterns always work?
options: No – that's why you use a stop
cards.explain: They shift odds, nothing more.

cards.prompt: One more: find the bearish engulfing

cards.title: Harami: the pregnant candle
cards.body: A harami is a large candle followed by a small one whose body fits inside the first body. The name is Japanese for 'pregnant'.

cards.title: What it says
cards.body: The strong move of the big candle stopped: the next period stayed inside it. After a drop, a bullish harami hints that selling is drying up – weaker than an engulfing.

cards.question: In a harami, the second body…
cards.explain: Small inside big – the opposite of engulfing.

cards.title: Inside bar
cards.body: An inside bar is a candle whose whole range – wicks included – sits inside the previous candle's range. It shows a pause and contraction.

cards.title: Trading the break
cards.body: Some traders wait for price to break the mother candle's high or low and follow that direction, with a stop on the other side. False breaks are common, so size small.

cards.question: Previous candle: high 60, low 50. Which next candle is an inside bar?
cards.explain: 53–58 is fully inside 50–60.

cards.question: Compared with a bullish engulfing, a bullish harami is usually…
cards.explain: A pause is less than a takeover.

cards.title: Harami cross
cards.body: When the small second candle is a doji, the pattern is called a harami cross. The pause is even more complete – but it still needs the next candles to show direction.

lessons.title: Piercing line and dark cloud cover

cards.title: Piercing line
cards.body: After a drop: a long red candle, then a green candle that opens below the red close and closes above the middle of the red body. Buyers took back more than half the loss.

cards.question: In a piercing line, the green candle closes…
options: Above the middle of the red body
cards.explain: More than halfway into the red body.

cards.title: Dark cloud cover
cards.body: The mirror after a rise: a long green candle, then a red candle that opens above the green close and closes below the middle of the green body.

cards.title: Halfway is the key
cards.body: If the second candle closes beyond the whole first body, it becomes an engulfing pattern – stronger. If it closes before the halfway point, the pattern is weak.

cards.question: Green body 40→50. The next red candle closes at 43. This is…
cards.explain: 43 is below the midpoint (45) but above the open (40).

cards.title: Gaps in 24/7 markets
cards.body: These patterns assume a gap at the open. In crypto, which trades nonstop, gaps are rare, so traders apply the idea loosely: the key is how deep the second candle reaches.

cards.question: Red body 60→50. Next green closes at 61. Which pattern is it really?
cards.explain: It closed above the whole red body.

cards.question: A dark cloud cover is a warning for…
cards.explain: Sellers pushed deep into the buyers' candle.

cards.title: Two candles, one level
cards.body: A tweezer bottom is two candles with (almost) the same low after a drop. Price tested a level twice and was rejected twice.

cards.title: Tweezer top
cards.body: Two candles with matching highs after a rise: buyers hit the same ceiling twice. Often the first is green and the second red.

cards.question: A tweezer bottom is defined by…
options: Two matching lows after a drop
cards.explain: The same low rejected twice.

cards.title: Better with a shape
cards.body: Tweezers become more convincing when combined with another signal: the second candle is a hammer, or the pair forms an engulfing.

cards.title: Exactness
cards.body: 'Matching' means very close relative to the candles' size – a few cents on a $50 stock. In practice, you're looking at a level that held, which leads to support and resistance in module 4.

cards.question: Two candles after a rise both reach a high of 75.02 and 75.00, then fall. This is…
cards.explain: Matching highs after a rise.

cards.question: What makes a tweezer bottom stronger?
options: The second candle is a hammer
cards.explain: Two signals together beat one.

cards.title: Where the stop goes
cards.body: With a tweezer bottom, the shared low is the line in the sand: a stop goes a little below it. If that low breaks, the double rejection has failed.

cards.title: Three candles
cards.body: A morning star forms after a drop: (1) a long red candle, (2) a small candle that shows hesitation, (3) a long green candle that closes well into the first candle's body.

cards.title: The story in three acts
cards.body: Sellers dominate, then they run out of strength and the market pauses, then buyers take control. Three candles tell a fuller story than one.

cards.question: The middle candle of a morning star is usually…
cards.explain: It shows the selling losing steam.

cards.title: Evening star
cards.body: The mirror after a rise: a long green candle, a small hesitant candle, then a long red candle closing deep into the green body.

cards.question: An evening star appears…
options: After a rise, warning of a top
After a drop, hinting at a bottom
cards.explain: Evening = the day (rally) is ending.

cards.title: Why three-candle patterns help
cards.body: The third candle is built-in confirmation: you don't act on the pause alone but on the strong move that follows it. The cost: a later entry and a wider stop.

cards.question: What is the trade-off of waiting for the third candle?
cards.explain: Confirmation costs part of the move.

cards.question: In an evening star, the third candle is…
cards.explain: Sellers take over after the pause.

cards.title: Three white soldiers
cards.body: Three long green candles in a row, each opening within the previous body and closing near its high. It shows steady, determined buying.

cards.title: Three black crows
cards.body: The mirror: three long red candles in a row, each closing near its low. Steady, determined selling.

cards.question: Three white soldiers show…
cards.explain: Three strong closes near the highs.

cards.title: Strength can also mean 'stretched'
cards.body: After a long run, three huge candles can mean the move is overextended and buyers are exhausted. Where it appears matters more than the shape.

cards.title: Watch the wicks
cards.body: If the soldiers start showing long upper wicks and shrinking bodies, buyers are struggling. Strength that fades is a warning even inside a strong pattern.

cards.question: Three big green candles appear after a 40% run in a few days. They may signal…
cards.explain: Late in a move, strength can mean exhaustion.

cards.question: Three red candles, each closing near its low, after a long rise. This is…
cards.explain: Steady selling after a rise.

cards.title: Out of a bottom vs. after a run
cards.body: Soldiers rising out of a long, quiet bottom suggest a new trend may be starting. The same three candles after a vertical run are more likely a late, tired move.

cards.title: Momentum candles
cards.body: A candle two or three times bigger than the recent average, closing near its extreme, often marks the start of a strong move – or a climax at its end.

cards.title: Gaps between candles
cards.body: On stocks, a candle can open far from the previous close, leaving an empty space on the chart. Gaps show that something changed overnight – usually news.

cards.question: A stock closed at 40 and opened at 44 after news. On the chart you see…
cards.explain: An empty space between 40 and 44.

cards.title: Gaps that fill and gaps that run
cards.body: Some gaps 'fill' – price returns to the previous close. Others run and never look back. A common belief that 'all gaps get filled' is not true.

cards.question: Is it true that every gap gets filled?
cards.explain: A popular myth. Treat gaps case by case.

cards.title: Climax candles
cards.body: A giant candle on giant volume after a long trend can be the last burst: everyone who wanted in got in. The next candles tell you whether it was a start or an end.

cards.question: A giant candle on huge volume after a long trend may be…
options: A climax near the end of the move
cards.explain: Late huge candles can be exhaustion.

cards.question: Early in a new move, a candle 3× the average closes at its high. This suggests…
cards.explain: Early big candles often start moves; late ones often end them.

cards.title: Wait for the next candle
cards.body: Many traders don't act on the pattern candle itself. They wait for the next candle to confirm – for a hammer, a candle that closes above the hammer's high.

cards.question: What confirms a hammer for many traders?
options: A next candle closing above its high
A next candle closing below its low
cards.explain: Buyers follow through.

cards.title: The trade-off
cards.body: Confirmation filters out some failures, but the entry is higher and the stop further away. There is no free lunch: you trade fewer losers for a worse price.

cards.title: Stops beyond the wick
cards.body: A logical stop goes just beyond the pattern's extreme – below the low for bullish patterns, above the high for bearish ones – plus a small buffer for noise.

cards.question: Bearish engulfing, pattern high 82. A logical stop for a short is…
cards.explain: Beyond the extreme, with a small buffer.

cards.title: Know your risk before you enter
cards.body: Entry minus stop = risk per share. If that distance is too big for your account, the trade is too big – skip it or trade fewer shares. Module 6 covers this in depth.

cards.question: Entry 50, stop 48. Risk per share is…
Waiting for confirmation usually means…
options: Fewer failures, but a worse entry
A better price and fewer failures
cards.explain: Every filter has a cost.

cards.title: Odds, not certainties
cards.body: Even good setups fail often. If a pattern works 55% of the time, it fails 45% of the time – and you can't know in advance which one you're looking at.

cards.question: A setup works 60% of the time. Out of 10 trades, how many losers is normal?
cards.explain: 40% losers on average, and streaks happen.

cards.title: Losing streaks are normal
cards.body: Even with a 60% win rate, five losses in a row will happen over a few hundred trades. Plan your risk so a streak can't knock you out.

cards.title: A failed pattern is information
cards.body: When a bullish pattern fails and price breaks its low, buyers who trusted it are trapped and must sell. Failed signals can produce sharp moves the other way.

cards.question: A hammer's low breaks the next day. What does it usually mean?
options: The signal failed – exit as planned
cards.explain: The buyers' defense broke.

cards.title: Sample size
cards.body: Three wins in a row prove nothing; neither do three losses. Judge a setup over dozens of examples. The Chart Trainer lets you practice hundreds of them safely.

cards.question: You tried a pattern 4 times and lost 3. The best conclusion is…
options: Trade it bigger to win back
cards.explain: Four trades is noise.

cards.title: Survive the streaks
cards.body: If each loss costs 1% of your account, ten losses in a row cost about 10% – painful but survivable. At 10% per trade, the same streak ends the account.

cards.title: Step 1: the trend
cards.body: Is the market rising, falling or sideways on your main timeframe? Reversal patterns need a trend; in a range, most single candles are noise.

cards.title: Step 2: the location
cards.body: Is the pattern at a meaningful level – a previous high or low? Patterns at levels deserve attention; patterns in the middle deserve skepticism.

cards.title: Step 3: the pattern
cards.body: Name it, and check the details: wick at least twice the body for a hammer, full body coverage for an engulfing, close past the midpoint for a piercing line.

cards.question: What should you check before naming the pattern?
cards.explain: Context first.

cards.title: Step 4: confirmation and risk
cards.body: Decide whether you need a confirming candle, where the stop goes, and whether that risk fits your account. If any answer is unclear, there is no trade.

cards.question: Everything looks good, but you can't find a logical stop. You…
cards.explain: No defined risk, no trade.

cards.prompt: Practice: find the Hammer
Practice: find the bullish engulfing

cards.question: The right order is…
cards.explain: From the big picture down to the trade.

exam.question: OHLC stands for…
exam.explain: The four prices of a candle.

exam.question: A close near the low of the candle shows…
exam.explain: Where it closes tells who won.

exam.question: Top-down reading starts with…
A Hammer appears…
A hammer shape after a long rise is called…
A dragonfly doji has…
options: A long lower wick, open and close at the high

exam.question: A bearish engulfing appears…
exam.explain: It warns the rise may end.

exam.question: A morning star has how many candles?
exam.explain: Big red, small pause, big green.

exam.question: For a bullish pattern, the logical stop goes…
Do candle patterns always work?
options: No – that's why you use a stop

modules.title: Scam protection
modules.subtitle: Spot the traps before they cost you

cards.title: How they work
cards.body: Telegram or WhatsApp groups post 'buy now' calls, show screenshots of wins, and sell a 'VIP' upgrade. Losses are rarely posted.

cards.title: Red flags
cards.body: Pressure to act fast, screenshots instead of a verified track record, no license, and the admin earning from your trades or subscriptions.

cards.question: Which is the biggest red flag?
options: A licensed firm's name and number
cards.explain: Urgency is the classic pressure tactic.

cards.title: The rule
cards.body: Personal investment advice requires a license in most countries, including Israel. An anonymous group with 'sure signals' is not advice – it's marketing.

cards.title: How the admin really earns
cards.body: Common models: monthly VIP fees, commissions from a broker for every member who signs up, or buying before posting the 'signal' and selling to the members who follow.

cards.question: A group admin gets paid by a broker for every member who opens an account. His 'signals' are…
options: Marketing with a conflict of interest
cards.explain: He earns from your activity, not from your results.

cards.title: Why results look so good
cards.body: Post ten calls, publicize the three that worked, quietly delete the rest. Run several groups with opposite calls and promote the one that got lucky.

cards.question: Personal investment advice in Israel requires…
cards.explain: Licensing exists to protect clients.

cards.title: The scheme
cards.body: Organizers quietly buy a small, cheap coin or stock, hype it to followers, then sell into the buying frenzy. Late buyers are left holding the crash.

cards.title: Warning signs
cards.body: A tiny asset, sudden volume, coordinated posts ('to the moon'), and a countdown to 'the pump'. If you hear about it from the group, you are the exit liquidity.

cards.question: In a pump & dump, who usually loses?
cards.explain: Organizers sell to them at the top.

cards.title: Why small assets
cards.body: Moving a giant company takes billions. A tiny stock or coin with a thin order book can double on a few thousand dollars of buying – and collapse just as fast.

cards.title: What 'exit liquidity' means
cards.body: To sell a big position, someone must buy it. In a pump, the hype exists to create those buyers. The people reading the excitement are the product being sold to.

cards.question: If you hear about a pump from the group, you are likely…
cards.explain: By the time it's public, insiders are selling.

cards.title: It's illegal
cards.body: Coordinated price manipulation is a crime in regulated markets, and regulators prosecute pump organizers. In unregulated corners of crypto, victims often have no one to turn to.

cards.question: A classic pump target is…
cards.explain: Thin markets are easy to push.

cards.title: Too good to be true
cards.body: '10% a month, guaranteed' is impossible to sustain. Real investments carry risk; anyone promising otherwise is lying or running a Ponzi scheme.

cards.question: Someone guarantees 5% a week. This is most likely…
cards.explain: No legitimate investment guarantees that.

cards.title: The lifestyle trick
cards.body: Rented cars and luxury photos prove nothing about trading skill. Often the real income is selling courses to you.

cards.title: Ask how they really earn
cards.body: If someone truly made 10% a month, a small account would grow into a fortune within a few years. Why would they spend their days selling a $997 course?

cards.question: A guru's luxury photos prove…
cards.explain: Image is marketing, not a track record.

cards.title: Honest education looks different
cards.body: Real educators talk about losses, risk and boring discipline. They don't promise income, and they don't pressure you to decide today.

cards.question: 'Guaranteed monthly returns' usually signals…
cards.explain: High + guaranteed = red flag.

cards.question: Which sounds like honest trading education?
options: 'Most beginners lose; here's how to manage risk'
cards.explain: Honesty about risk is the tell.

cards.title: How a Ponzi works
cards.body: A Ponzi scheme pays 'returns' to early investors using money from new investors. There is no real trading behind it – only a growing hole.

cards.title: Why early payouts are the bait
cards.body: Early investors really do get paid, so they tell friends and invest more. The scheme needs ever more new money and collapses when it slows.

cards.question: Your friend has received 'returns' for six months. Does that prove it's legitimate?
cards.explain: Early payouts are the recruiting tool.

cards.title: Too smooth
cards.body: Real investments go up and down. A fund showing steady profits every single month, never a losing month, should worry you, not reassure you.

cards.title: Pyramids and 'trading academies'
cards.body: In a pyramid, you earn mainly by recruiting others, who must recruit more. Some 'trading clubs' are pyramids: the product is a course, the profit is recruitment.

cards.question: A 'trading club' pays you mainly for bringing new members. It is likely…
cards.explain: Income from recruiting, not from a real product.

cards.title: Withdrawal trouble
cards.body: A classic late sign: withdrawals are delayed, 'temporarily paused' or require a new fee. By then, the money is usually gone.

cards.question: Which return history is the biggest red flag?
options: +2% every month, never a losing month
cards.explain: Too smooth to be real.

lessons.title: Social media hype and paid promotion

cards.title: Finfluencers
cards.body: Many popular 'finance influencers' are paid to promote stocks, coins, brokers or apps. Some disclose it; many don't.

cards.title: Ask: who pays?
cards.body: Before trusting a recommendation, ask how the person earns. Paid promotions, affiliate links and owning the asset they praise all create a conflict of interest.

cards.question: An influencer praises a coin and gets paid by its project. Their opinion is…
cards.explain: Paid praise is an ad.

cards.title: Fake social proof
cards.body: Followers, likes and comments can be bought. Bots can make a coin look like everyone's talking about it. Popularity is not evidence.

cards.question: A coin's posts have thousands of identical comments: 'Great project! 🚀'. This suggests…
cards.explain: Identical comments are a bot signature.

cards.title: Deepfakes
cards.body: Scammers use AI to fake videos of celebrities, journalists or bank chiefs 'recommending' a platform. A famous face in an ad proves nothing.

cards.title: FOMO by design
cards.body: Feeds are built to make you feel everyone else is getting rich. That feeling – fear of missing out – is exactly what hype sellers target.

cards.question: A video shows a famous businessman praising a trading app. You should…
options: Assume it may be fake and verify independently
cards.explain: Deepfake endorsements are common.

cards.title: Screenshots are easy to fake
cards.body: A profit screenshot can be edited in seconds, taken from a demo account, or be the one winning trade out of fifty losers.

cards.question: Why is a profit screenshot weak evidence?
options: It can be edited, demo or cherry-picked
cards.explain: One image shows nothing about the full record.

cards.title: What a real track record looks like
cards.body: All trades, wins and losses, over a long period, verified by an independent party or a regulated fund's audited reports. Anything less is a story.

cards.title: Survivorship bias
cards.body: You hear from the few who won big, not the thousands who lost quietly. A thousand people flipping coins will produce a few 'geniuses' with ten heads in a row.

cards.question: 1,000 people make random trades; 5 have amazing years and start selling courses. This shows…
cards.explain: Luck produces winners too.

cards.title: The demo-account trick
cards.body: Some sellers show live trading from a demo account that looks identical to a real one, with fake money and no slippage. Ask for verified statements – they rarely appear.

cards.question: Which is real evidence of a trader's results?
options: All trades over years, independently verified
cards.explain: Complete, long and verified.

cards.question: You only see successful traders online because…
cards.explain: The losers are invisible.

cards.title: The fake broker
cards.body: A slick platform shows profits, encourages bigger deposits, then blocks withdrawals with 'fees' or 'taxes'. The money was never really traded.

cards.title: The numbers on screen aren't real
cards.body: The 'account balance' is just a number on their website. They can show any profit they want – it costs nothing to type.

cards.question: A platform asks for a 'tax' before you can withdraw. You should…
cards.explain: Legit brokers don't hold withdrawals hostage.

cards.title: The account manager
cards.body: A friendly 'account manager' calls often, celebrates your gains, and pushes you to deposit more – sometimes suggesting a loan. Real brokers don't do that.

cards.title: Small withdrawal first
cards.body: Some fake platforms let you withdraw a small amount early to build trust. It's bait for a much larger deposit later.

cards.question: Your 'account manager' suggests taking a loan to deposit more. This is…
cards.explain: Pressure to deposit more is the scheme itself.

cards.title: Check before you deposit
cards.body: Before sending any money, find the firm in a regulator's register (next lessons) and confirm the website and phone match the register's details exactly.

cards.question: Blocked withdrawals with new 'fees' indicate…
cards.explain: A classic sign of fraud.

cards.title: The second hit
cards.body: After a loss, 'recovery experts' promise to get your money back for an upfront fee. This is usually the same scammers again.

cards.title: How they find you
cards.body: Victim lists are sold between scam groups. If someone contacts you out of the blue knowing exactly what you lost, that knowledge is a warning sign, not a credential.

cards.question: A stranger offers to recover your lost money for a fee upfront. This is…
cards.explain: Upfront 'recovery' fees are a known scam.

cards.title: Fake officials
cards.body: Recovery scammers often pose as lawyers, police, regulators or 'blockchain investigators', with official-looking letters and logos.

cards.title: Real authorities don't charge
cards.body: Police and regulators do not ask victims to pay fees to release money, and they don't contact you through WhatsApp asking for crypto.

cards.question: A 'regulator' emails that your lost funds are found and asks for a release fee in crypto. This is…
options: A scam – regulators don't do this
cards.explain: Authorities never charge to release funds.

cards.title: Where real help is
cards.body: Contact your bank or card company, file a police report, and report to the regulator yourself – using contact details you looked up independently.

cards.question: Recovery 'experts' asking upfront fees are…
cards.explain: Don't pay twice.

cards.title: Clone firms
cards.body: Scammers copy the name, license number and logo of a real, regulated firm and build a near-identical website. The register says 'licensed' – but you're not talking to that firm.

cards.question: A website shows a real firm's license number. Is that enough?
options: No – it may be a clone
cards.explain: Verify the contact details through the register.

cards.title: Tiny differences
cards.body: Look for small changes: an extra letter in the web address, a different ending (.co instead of .com), a mobile number instead of an office line.

cards.title: Impersonating your bank
cards.body: 'This is your bank's security team – your account is under attack, move your money to a safe account.' No real bank ever asks you to move money to protect it.

cards.question: A caller from 'your bank' asks you to move money to a 'safe account'. You…
options: Hang up and call the bank's official number
cards.explain: Hang up, then call a number you looked up yourself.

cards.title: Caller ID lies
cards.body: Phone numbers and SMS sender names can be spoofed to look like your bank. A familiar name on the screen proves nothing.

cards.question: An SMS appears under your bank's name with a link. Is it safe?
options: Not necessarily – sender names can be faked
cards.explain: Open the bank's app yourself instead of the link.

cards.question: chartora-invest.co vs. chartora.com – the safe move is…
options: Use only the address listed in the regulator's register
cards.explain: The register is the source of truth.

cards.title: Check the regulator, not the website
cards.body: Look the firm or person up in the regulator's own public register: in Israel the Israel Securities Authority (ISA), in the UK the FCA register, in the US FINRA BrokerCheck and the SEC.

cards.question: Where should you verify a broker's license?
cards.explain: Only the regulator's register is reliable.

cards.title: Watch for clones
cards.body: Scammers copy real firms' names. Contact the firm using details from the regulator's register, never from the ad or message you received.

cards.title: Warning lists
cards.body: Many regulators also publish warning lists of firms known to operate without a license. A name on such a list is a clear stop sign.

cards.title: Which license?
cards.body: Check that the license covers what they offer you. A firm licensed for insurance isn't licensed to manage your trading account, and an offshore license may offer you almost no protection.

cards.question: In the US you can check a broker on…
cards.explain: BrokerCheck is FINRA's public tool.

cards.question: Contact a firm using details from…
cards.explain: Never from the ad or message.

cards.question: A firm appears on a regulator's warning list. You should…
cards.explain: A warning list is a stop sign.

cards.title: It starts with a 'wrong number'
cards.body: A friendly stranger messages by mistake, or matches with you on a dating app. Weeks of warm conversation follow – no mention of money.

cards.title: Then the 'opportunity'
cards.body: They mention that an uncle or mentor taught them a trading or crypto method, show their profits, and kindly offer to help you start on a 'platform'.

cards.question: An online friend you've never met in person urges you to invest on their platform. This is…
cards.explain: Trust is built first, then used.

cards.title: Why it's called 'pig butchering'
cards.body: The scammers' own term: they 'fatten' the victim with attention and small fake profits, then take everything. Many victims lose their life savings.

cards.title: Often victims on both sides
cards.body: Investigations have found that many of the people typing these messages are themselves trafficked and forced to work in scam compounds. The organizers stay hidden.

cards.question: What is the safest rule?
options: Never invest because an online contact suggested it
cards.explain: Small tests are part of the scam.

cards.title: Talk to someone
cards.body: Scammers ask you to keep it secret – 'your family won't understand'. Secrecy is a red flag. Telling one trusted person often breaks the spell.

cards.question: Your online friend says: 'Don't tell your family, they won't understand.' This is…
cards.explain: Isolation protects the scam.

cards.title: Fake login pages
cards.body: Phishing messages link to pages that look exactly like your broker, bank or exchange. Whatever you type – password, codes – goes straight to the scammer.

cards.question: An email says your broker account is locked and gives a login link. The safest move is…
cards.explain: Never log in through a link you were sent.

cards.title: Two-factor authentication
cards.body: Turn on two-factor authentication (2FA) everywhere money lives. An authenticator app is safer than SMS codes, which can be stolen by SIM swap.

cards.title: Never share a code
cards.body: A one-time code is the key to your account. No real support agent will ever ask you to read it out. Anyone asking for it is trying to break in.

cards.question: 'Support' calls and asks for the 6-digit code you just received. You…
cards.explain: The code is for you only.

cards.title: Password basics
cards.body: Use a different, long password for each financial account and a password manager to remember them. One leaked password shouldn't open every door.

cards.question: Which 2FA method is generally safest?
cards.explain: SMS can be hijacked by SIM swap.

cards.question: Why use a different password for each financial account?
cards.explain: Limit the damage of any single leak.

cards.title: 'Let me help you set it up'
cards.body: A caller offers to help you open an account or 'fix a problem' and asks you to install a screen-sharing app like AnyDesk or TeamViewer.

cards.title: What they do with it
cards.body: With remote access they can see your screen, read codes as they arrive, open your banking app and move money – while you watch or after you look away.

cards.question: A 'broker' asks you to install AnyDesk so they can help you trade. You…
cards.explain: Remote access = handing over your devices.

cards.title: Unsolicited calls
cards.body: Legit firms rarely cold-call people to sell investments. An unexpected call about an 'investment opportunity' is reason enough to hang up.

cards.title: If you already installed it
cards.body: Disconnect from the internet, uninstall the app, change passwords from another device, call your bank's official number, and check for new transfers or payees.

cards.question: You let a caller access your computer. First steps?
cards.explain: Speed matters – act immediately.

cards.question: An unexpected call offers an 'exclusive investment'. The best response is…
cards.explain: Cold calls about investments are a warning sign.

cards.title: Your devices are your vault
cards.body: Nobody needs to see your screen to help you invest. Treat requests for access the way you would treat a stranger asking for your house keys.

cards.title: 'Send 1, get 2 back'
cards.body: Fake giveaways – often with a hacked or deepfaked celebrity account – promise to double any crypto you send. Nothing ever comes back.

cards.question: A celebrity account promises to double any Bitcoin you send. This is…
cards.explain: No one doubles your money for free.

cards.title: Wallet drainers
cards.body: A fake mint, airdrop or 'claim' page asks you to connect your wallet and sign a transaction. That signature can give permission to empty the wallet.

cards.title: Read before you sign
cards.body: Never sign something you don't understand, especially 'approve' or 'set approval for all'. Keep most funds in a wallet that never connects to new sites.

cards.question: A site you found in a DM asks you to sign 'approve all' to claim free tokens. You…
cards.explain: Free tokens + approval request = drainer.

cards.title: Fake exchanges and apps
cards.body: Fake crypto exchanges and copycat wallet apps exist in app stores and ads. Download only from the official site, and check the publisher and reviews carefully.

cards.question: Where should most of your crypto sit?
options: In a wallet that never connects to new sites
In the wallet you use for every airdrop
cards.explain: Separate your vault from your experiments.

cards.title: No undo button
cards.body: Crypto transfers are usually irreversible. Once coins leave your wallet, there is no bank to call to reverse them. Slow down before every transfer.

cards.title: The pitch
cards.body: 'Our AI bot trades for you 24/7 and makes 2% a day.' Ads for automated systems promise passive income with no effort and no risk.

cards.question: A bot 'reliably' earns 2% a day. Compounded for a year that would be…
cards.explain: 1.02^365 is in the thousands. Nobody sells that.

cards.title: The usual reality
cards.body: Many 'bots' are a front: there's no algorithm, just a fake dashboard. Others are real software that loses money, sold with backtests tuned to look perfect.

cards.title: Backtests can lie
cards.body: It's easy to tweak a system until it would have been perfect on past data. That's called overfitting, and it usually fails on new data.

cards.question: A bot shows a flawless 5-year backtest. The main risk is…
cards.explain: Perfect on the past ≠ good in the future.

cards.title: Who holds the money?
cards.body: If you must send money to the bot company rather than keep it at your own licensed broker, you're trusting them with everything. That's the real product.

cards.question: A bot service asks you to deposit money directly with them. This means…
options: They control your money – high risk
cards.explain: Custody is where the risk lives.

cards.title: Real automation is boring
cards.body: Professional algorithmic trading needs large teams, data and infrastructure – and it still has losing years. Anyone selling certainty for $299 is selling a story.

cards.title: Account management offers
cards.body: Someone offers to trade your account for a share of the profits, asking for your login. Managing other people's money requires a license – and your login is yours alone.

cards.question: A trader offers to manage your account if you share your password. You…
cards.explain: Sharing a login gives away full control.

cards.title: Profit share = risk incentive
cards.body: If someone earns a big cut of profits but loses nothing on losses, their incentive is to take huge risks with your money.

cards.title: Copy trading
cards.body: Some platforms let you automatically copy other traders. Remember: leaderboards show recent winners, and recent winners often took big risks that haven't blown up yet.

cards.question: A copy-trading star is up 300% this year. What should worry you?
options: Such returns usually mean huge risk
cards.explain: Extreme returns come from extreme risk.

cards.title: Legitimate options exist
cards.body: Licensed portfolio managers and regulated funds exist, with reports, oversight and your money held at a custodian. Check the license, the fees and who holds the money.

cards.question: What makes a managed account more trustworthy?
options: A license and money held at a custodian
cards.explain: Structure beats charm.

cards.question: Someone takes 50% of profits and nothing of losses. Their incentive is to…
options: Take big risks with your money
cards.explain: Heads they win, tails you lose.

cards.title: Scams target feelings, not logic
