cards.body: Scammers don't need you to be stupid – they need you to be rushed, excited or afraid. Smart people get scammed every day.

cards.title: Urgency and scarcity
cards.body: 'Only today', 'last 3 spots', 'price goes up at midnight'. Time pressure stops you from checking. Real opportunities survive a 24-hour pause.

cards.question: 'Price doubles at midnight – decide now!' The best response is…
cards.explain: Pressure is the tell.

cards.title: Authority and social proof
cards.body: Uniforms, titles, logos and 'thousands of happy members' make us trust. Each can be faked. Check facts, not appearances.

cards.title: Sunk cost
cards.body: After paying once, people pay again to 'protect' what they already paid. Scammers know this and invent new fees. Money already lost shouldn't drive the next decision.

cards.question: You paid a $500 'fee' to withdraw. Now they ask for $2,000 more. The trap is…
options: Sunk cost – paying to save earlier payments
cards.explain: Stop paying. The money isn't coming back through them.

cards.title: Your defense: a pause rule
cards.body: Make it a rule: no financial decision on the same day as the pitch, and talk to one trusted person first. Most scams fall apart under a calm 24 hours.

cards.question: Which tactic is NOT a pressure tactic?
options: Giving you written terms to review at home
cards.explain: Time to think is what honest offers give.

cards.title: 'I have inside info'
cards.body: A real insider tip – non-public information about a company – is illegal to trade on in regulated markets. A fake tip is a scam. Either way, it's a trap.

cards.question: A friend's cousin 'knows' about a merger before it's announced. Trading on it is…
cards.explain: Non-public material information = insider trading.

cards.title: Fake news moves prices
cards.body: Manipulators spread false rumors – a fake takeover, a fake partnership, a fake 'approval' – to move a price they've positioned for. Check the company's official filings.

cards.title: Spoofing and wash trading
cards.body: Spoofing: placing large fake orders to fake demand, then cancelling. Wash trading: trading with yourself to fake volume. Both are illegal in regulated markets and common in unregulated ones.

cards.question: Huge buy orders appear in the book and vanish just before price reaches them. This may be…
cards.explain: Fake orders create fake demand.

cards.title: Volume can be fake too
cards.body: On small, unregulated exchanges, reported volume can be inflated many times over. Be skeptical of a tiny coin showing huge 'volume' on one obscure venue.

cards.question: A tiny coin shows enormous volume on a single unknown exchange. You should suspect…
cards.explain: Fake volume makes fake liquidity.

cards.question: A rumor says a company got a big contract. Where do you check?
cards.explain: Primary sources beat rumors.

cards.title: Stop paying
cards.body: The first step is the hardest: stop sending money, no matter what they promise or threaten. Every new payment only adds to the loss.

cards.title: Call your bank immediately
cards.body: Contact your bank or credit card company at once. Card payments and some transfers can sometimes be disputed or stopped – but speed matters.

cards.question: You realize you were scammed an hour ago by card payment. First call?
options: A recovery service from an ad
cards.explain: The faster the bank knows, the better the chances.

cards.title: Document everything
cards.body: Save messages, emails, website addresses, wallet addresses, transaction IDs and dates. Don't delete the chats, even if you're embarrassed.

cards.title: Report it
cards.body: File a police report, report to the securities regulator and, in Israel, cyber incidents to the National Cyber Directorate's 119 hotline. Reports help stop the next victim.

cards.question: Why keep the scam chats instead of deleting them?
options: They're evidence for the bank and police
cards.explain: Evidence helps every report.

cards.title: Secure your accounts
cards.body: Change passwords, turn on 2FA, remove any remote-access apps, and watch your accounts. Then expect 'recovery' offers – and ignore them.

cards.title: No shame
cards.body: Scams are run by professionals and organized groups. Being targeted says nothing about your intelligence. Talking about it protects others.

cards.question: After reporting, you get a call offering to recover your money for a fee. It's most likely…
cards.explain: Recovery scams follow victims.

cards.title: 1. Who are they?
cards.body: Find them in a regulator's register and contact them only through the details listed there. No license, no money.

cards.title: 2. What are they promising?
cards.body: High returns, guaranteed, fast, with no risk – any one of these is a warning; together they are a scam.

cards.question: Which promise alone should make you stop?
cards.explain: Guarantees are the hallmark of fraud.

cards.title: 3. How are they pushing?
cards.body: Urgency, secrecy, flattery, requests to install apps or share codes, or to pay in crypto or gift cards. Each is a reason to stop.

cards.title: 4. Who holds the money?
cards.body: Your money should stay at a licensed institution in your name. Sending it to a person, a private wallet or an unknown platform means giving it away.

cards.question: Which payment request is the biggest red flag?
options: Pay in gift cards or crypto to a person
A transfer to your own licensed broker
A card payment to your bank
cards.explain: Untraceable payments to people = scam.

cards.title: 5. Sleep on it
cards.body: Wait 24 hours and tell one trusted person. If it's real, it will still be there tomorrow. If it's a scam, the pressure will show itself.

cards.question: Which habit protects you most?
cards.explain: Verification plus time beats almost every scam.

exam.question: 'Signal' groups usually post…
If you hear about a pump from the group, you are likely…
A Ponzi scheme pays returns from…
exam.explain: Old investors are paid with new money.

exam.question: Seeing only successful traders online is an example of…
Blocked withdrawals with new 'fees' indicate…
A site shows a real firm's license number. To be safe you…
options: Contact the firm via the register's details
Call the number on the site

exam.question: An online friend pushes you to invest on their platform. This is…
Someone asks for the one-time code you just received. You…
A caller asks you to install a screen-sharing app. You…
Recovery 'experts' asking upfront fees are…

modules.title: Trends, support & resistance
modules.subtitle: Draw the map before you trade

cards.title: Three directions
cards.body: An uptrend makes higher highs and higher lows. A downtrend makes lower highs and lower lows. Anything else is a range: price moving sideways. Name the direction before you look at anything else.

cards.title: Drawing a trend line
cards.body: In an uptrend, connect at least two rising lows and extend the line to the right. In a downtrend, connect falling highs. A third touch that holds makes the line more meaningful.

cards.title: Pick the right timeframe
cards.body: An uptrend on a 5-minute chart can be a small bounce inside a daily downtrend. Many traders check a higher timeframe first, then zoom in to plan the details.

cards.title: When the line breaks
cards.body: A close beyond a trend line says the trend may be weakening. It does not prove a reversal. A reversal is clearer when the structure changes too: an uptrend that starts making lower highs and lower lows.

cards.prompt: Draw the trend line: tap two lows that the line should connect.
cards.explain: An uptrend line runs through rising lows that price respected. The lows here bounced right on it.

cards.question: Higher highs and higher lows describe…
cards.explain: Rising highs and rising lows are the definition of an uptrend.

cards.question: What is the minimum to draw a trend line?
cards.explain: Two points make a line; a third touch that holds makes it more meaningful.

cards.title: Steep lines break first
cards.body: A very steep trend line is hard to sustain; price usually breaks it and settles into a gentler slope. A break of a steep line often means 'slower', not 'over'.

cards.question: A steep trend line breaks, but the lows are still rising. Most likely…
options: The trend is slowing, not necessarily over
cards.explain: Structure (rising lows) still says uptrend.

cards.title: Swing highs and swing lows
cards.body: A swing high is a peak with lower candles on both sides; a swing low is a dip with higher candles on both sides. They are the skeleton of every chart.

cards.title: Reading the sequence
cards.body: Label each swing: HH (higher high), HL (higher low), LH (lower high), LL (lower low). HH + HL = uptrend. LH + LL = downtrend. A mix = range or transition.

cards.question: The last swings are LH, LL, LH, LL. The structure is…
cards.explain: Lower highs and lower lows.

cards.prompt: Look at the swings. What is the structure?
cards.explain: Each low is higher than the last, and so is each high: an uptrend.

cards.title: Ignore the noise
cards.body: Not every wiggle is a swing. Focus on the clear turning points you'd notice from arm's length. Too many labels hide the picture.

cards.title: Structure before indicators
cards.body: Structure is the raw price story. Indicators (module 5) are calculations on top of it. When they disagree, many traders trust structure first.

cards.question: A swing low is…
options: A dip with higher candles on both sides
cards.explain: A local turning point.

cards.question: HH, HL, HH, then a LL. What changed?
cards.explain: A lower low breaks the chain of higher lows.

cards.title: Trends move in waves
cards.body: No trend goes straight. An uptrend is a series of pushes up and pullbacks down. The pullbacks are where the higher lows are made.

cards.title: Healthy vs. weak pullbacks
cards.body: In a strong trend, pullbacks are short and shallow and the pushes are big. When pullbacks get deeper and pushes smaller, the trend is tiring.

cards.question: Each push up is smaller and each pullback deeper. The trend is…
cards.explain: Momentum is fading.

cards.prompt: Draw the downtrend line: tap two highs that the line should connect.
cards.explain: A downtrend line connects falling highs. Each rally stalled at or below it.

cards.title: Buying the dip is not a strategy by itself
cards.body: A pullback in an uptrend can be an opportunity – or the start of a reversal. Traders wait for signs the pullback is ending, like a higher low forming, and still use a stop.

cards.title: Measuring depth
cards.body: A simple way: compare a pullback with the push before it. Giving back a third is common; giving back almost everything puts the trend in doubt.

cards.question: Price rose from 100 to 130, then fell back to 128. That pullback is…
cards.explain: Giving back 2 of 30 points is very shallow.

cards.question: Where is a higher low created in an uptrend?
options: At the end of a pullback
At the top of a push
cards.explain: Pullbacks end at higher lows.

cards.title: Two parallel lines
cards.body: A channel is a trend line plus a parallel line on the other side. In an up-channel, the lower line connects lows and the upper line touches the highs.

cards.title: What traders watch
cards.body: Moves toward the lower line in an up-channel are where buyers have stepped in before. The upper line shows where rallies have stalled.

cards.question: In an up-channel, the upper line is drawn through…
options: The highs, parallel to the lower trend line
cards.explain: Two parallel lines frame the trend.

cards.prompt: Draw the lower channel line: tap two lows.
cards.explain: The lower line of an up-channel is the trend line through rising lows.

cards.title: Failing to reach the top
cards.body: When rallies stop well short of the upper line, buyers are weakening. A close below the lower line then becomes more significant.

cards.title: Channels are approximate
cards.body: Real markets don't respect lines to the cent. Treat channel lines as zones, and expect overshoots and undershoots.

cards.question: Rallies in an up-channel stop far below the upper line. This suggests…
cards.explain: Shorter pushes = less buying power.

cards.question: How should you treat channel lines?
cards.explain: Lines are maps, not walls.

cards.title: Floors and ceilings
cards.body: Support is a price area where falls have stopped before, because buyers showed up. Resistance is an area where rises have stopped, because sellers showed up. Think of zones, not exact lines.

cards.title: Why they work
cards.body: Traders remember prices. People who missed the last bounce wait to buy at the same level. People stuck in a losing trade want to sell when price returns to their entry.

cards.title: Role reversal
cards.body: When resistance breaks, it often turns into support when price comes back to test it. Broken support often turns into resistance. Traders call this a retest.

cards.title: Many touches, weaker level?
cards.body: Each touch uses up orders waiting at the level. A level hit again and again in a short time is more likely to give way. Old levels on higher timeframes usually matter more than fresh ones on tiny timeframes.

cards.prompt: Drag the line onto the support zone.
cards.explain: Support is where falls stopped again and again: here, three bounces from the same zone.

cards.question: Price fell to 50 three times and bounced each time. 50 is…
cards.explain: Falls stopped there because buyers appeared: support.

cards.question: Resistance at 80 breaks, then price returns to 80. What often happens?
cards.explain: Broken resistance often becomes support on a retest. Often, not always.

cards.question: Should support be drawn as a single exact price?
cards.explain: Orders cluster around an area.

cards.title: Levels from the past
cards.body: Support and resistance come from where price turned before. Scroll left: the old turning points are your candidates for the next reaction.

cards.title: Start from clear turns
cards.body: Mark the obvious swing highs and lows first. A good level is one where price turned sharply, ideally more than once.

cards.title: Wicks or bodies?
cards.body: Some traders draw at the wicks, others at the bodies. A practical approach: draw a zone that covers both – from the body closes to the wick tips.

cards.question: Wick tips at 50.2, body closes at 50.8. A practical support zone is…
cards.explain: A zone covers both wicks and bodies.

cards.prompt: Drag the line onto the resistance zone.
cards.explain: Resistance is the ceiling where rallies kept stalling – here, the tops of the range.

cards.title: Less is more
cards.body: A chart covered in 15 lines is useless: price is always 'near a level'. Keep the two or three most obvious levels around the current price.

cards.title: Recent beats ancient
cards.body: A level price reacted to last month usually matters more than one from five years ago, unless the old one is a major multi-year high or low.

cards.question: Your chart has 14 horizontal lines. The best fix is…
cards.explain: Clarity beats coverage.

cards.question: What makes a level stronger?
options: Sharp turns there, more than once
cards.explain: Clear, repeated reactions.

cards.title: Psychological levels
cards.body: Round numbers – 100, 50, $1,000, Bitcoin at 100,000 – attract orders because people like them for targets and stops. Price often reacts around them.

cards.question: Why do round numbers often act as levels?
cards.explain: Human habits create clusters.

cards.title: Stops just past the round number
cards.body: Because many stops sit just below 100 or just above it, price can poke through briefly to trigger them. Placing your stop a little further away can avoid the crowd.

cards.title: Previous day, week, month
cards.body: The previous day's high and low, and the previous week's, are watched by many traders. Breaking yesterday's high is a common short-term signal.

cards.question: Which level do many short-term traders watch?
cards.explain: Widely watched levels become self-fulfilling at times.

cards.title: All-time highs
cards.body: At an all-time high there is no resistance from the past – nobody is stuck in a losing trade above. Moves there can be fast, in both directions.

cards.question: Your stop for a long is at exactly 100.00, a round number. A risk is…
options: A quick poke below 100 triggers many stops, including yours
cards.explain: Crowded stops get hunted by volatility.

cards.question: At an all-time high, overhead resistance from past trades is…
cards.explain: No one bought higher – there are no stuck sellers.

cards.title: Sideways is common
cards.body: Markets spend a lot of time going nowhere: price bounces between a support floor and a resistance ceiling. That is a range.

cards.title: Edges matter, the middle doesn't
cards.body: Inside a range, the edges are where reactions happen. The middle is no-man's-land: risk and reward are both unclear there.

cards.question: Price is exactly in the middle of a range. Typically this is…
options: The least clear place to act
cards.explain: No edge in the middle.

cards.prompt: Mark the floor of this range: drag the line onto support.
cards.explain: The floor is where each drop stopped and turned up.

cards.title: Trend tools fail in ranges
cards.body: Breakout and trend-following methods get chopped up in ranges: every 'break' reverses. Recognizing a range is a reason to change approach or wait.

cards.title: Ranges end
cards.body: Every range eventually breaks. The longer it lasts, the more orders build up at its edges – which can make the eventual move bigger.

cards.question: Trend-following signals keep failing. The market might be…
cards.explain: Ranges chop trend methods.

cards.question: A long range has finally broken. Compared with a short range, the move may be…
cards.explain: More stored orders, more fuel – no guarantee.

cards.title: What a breakout is
cards.body: A breakout is a close beyond a support or resistance zone or a pattern line. Real breakouts often come with a jump in volume as many traders act at once.

cards.title: The trap
cards.body: Many breakouts fail. Price pokes above resistance, triggers buy orders and stop-losses, then falls back inside the range. This is a false breakout, or 'fakeout'.

cards.title: How traders filter
cards.body: Common filters: wait for a candle to close beyond the level, not just a wick; look for rising volume; or wait for price to come back and hold the broken level.

cards.title: Plan for failure
cards.body: Because breakouts can fail, traders decide in advance where the idea is wrong, often just back inside the old range. The Chart Trainer shows failed patterns on purpose, so you get used to them.

cards.prompt: Tap the candle that broke out above resistance.
cards.explain: The breakout is the first candle that closed clearly above the old ceiling, not just a wick through it.

cards.prompt: What happened after price went above resistance?
cards.explain: Price closed above resistance, then fell back inside the range: a false breakout.

cards.question: Which is a stronger sign of a real breakout?
options: A close beyond the level with rising volume
A post saying it will break
cards.explain: A close plus volume shows real participation. A wick alone often fails.

cards.question: Price breaks above resistance, then closes back below it. This is…
cards.explain: It broke out, then failed back into the range.

cards.question: Who gets trapped in a false breakout above resistance?
cards.explain: They must sell as price falls back – fueling the drop.

cards.title: The retest
cards.body: After a breakout above resistance, price often comes back to the broken level. If it holds as support, the breakout looks more genuine.

cards.prompt: Tap the breakout candle: the first clear close above resistance.
cards.explain: The close above the ceiling marks the break; a retest, if it comes, is the next test of that level.

cards.title: Why traders like it
cards.body: Entering on the retest gives a clearer stop – just below the old resistance – and avoids chasing a candle that has already run far.

cards.question: After breaking 80, price returns to 80 and bounces. This is…
cards.explain: Old resistance acting as new support.

cards.title: The catch
cards.body: Strong breakouts often don't come back at all. Waiting for a retest means sometimes missing the move. Every method has a price.

cards.title: When the retest fails
cards.body: If price falls back through the level and closes inside the old range, the breakout has failed. That's usually a clear exit signal for those who bought it.

cards.question: Where does a logical stop go when entering on a retest of broken resistance?
options: A little below the old resistance
cards.explain: If the level fails as support, the idea is wrong.

cards.question: What's the trade-off of waiting for a retest?
options: Sometimes the move leaves without you
cards.explain: Patience costs some missed moves.

cards.title: The first warning: a lower high
cards.body: In an uptrend, the first rally that fails to make a new high is a warning. Buyers couldn't push as far as last time.

cards.title: The confirmation: breaking the last higher low
cards.body: When price then falls below the most recent higher low, the uptrend structure is broken. Many traders treat this as the trend's end, at least for now.

cards.question: Uptrend: last higher low at 90. Price closes at 88. What happened?
cards.explain: A lower low ends the HH/HL chain.

cards.prompt: Compare the last peak with the one before it. What does it show?
cards.explain: The right shoulder is lower than the head: a lower high, the first warning. The break below the neckline confirmed it.

cards.title: Not every break is a reversal
cards.body: After the uptrend ends, the market may turn down – or just move sideways for a while. 'The uptrend ended' doesn't mean 'a downtrend started'.

cards.title: Protecting gains
cards.body: For someone holding a long position, these signs are reasons to tighten stops or take profits. Waiting for a full downtrend to be 'confirmed' can give back a lot.

cards.question: An uptrend's structure just broke. The most accurate statement is…
options: The uptrend ended; the next phase is unknown
cards.explain: Down or sideways – both are possible.

cards.question: Which comes first in a typical top?
cards.explain: Failure to rise, then failure to hold.

cards.title: The shape
cards.body: After an uptrend: a peak (left shoulder), a higher peak (head), then a lower peak (right shoulder). It shows buyers failing to push to new highs.

cards.title: The neckline
cards.body: The neckline connects the lows between the three peaks. The pattern is only complete when price closes below the neckline. Before that, it is just a possibility.

cards.title: A rough measured move
cards.body: Traders often take the distance from the head down to the neckline and project it down from the break. It is an estimate of room to move, not a promise.

cards.title: The inverse version
cards.body: Upside down after a downtrend, it is an inverse head and shoulders. It completes on a close above the neckline. Both versions fail regularly, so a plan for being wrong still matters.

cards.prompt: Drag the line onto the neckline.
cards.explain: The neckline runs through the two lows between the shoulders and the head. The pattern completed when price closed below it.

cards.question: When is a head and shoulders complete?
options: When price closes below the neckline
cards.explain: Until the neckline breaks, it is only a possible pattern.

cards.question: Head at 120, neckline at 100. A common rough target after the break is…
cards.explain: 120 − 100 = 20, projected down from 100 → about 80. An estimate, not a promise.

cards.question: Before the neckline breaks, a head and shoulders is…
cards.explain: Many 'almost' patterns never complete.

cards.title: Double top
cards.body: Price rises to a high, pulls back, rallies to about the same high again and fails. The low between the two peaks is the key level.

cards.title: Completion
cards.body: Like head and shoulders, a double top is only complete when price closes below the low between the peaks. Until then, it may just be a pause in an uptrend.

cards.question: Two peaks at 150, the low between them at 135. The double top completes when…
cards.explain: The middle low is the trigger.

cards.title: Double bottom
cards.body: The mirror after a drop: two lows at about the same price, with a peak between them. It completes on a close above that peak.

cards.title: A rough target
cards.body: Traders often project the pattern's height from the break: for peaks at 150 and a middle low at 135, about 15 points below 135. An estimate, not a promise.

cards.question: Peaks at 150, middle low 135. A rough measured target after the break is…
cards.explain: Height 15, projected from 135.

cards.prompt: This range shows repeated tops at the same ceiling. Drag the line onto it.
cards.explain: Repeated failures at one ceiling are the raw material of double and triple tops.

cards.question: A double bottom completes when price…
options: Closes above the peak between the lows
cards.explain: The middle peak is the trigger.

cards.title: Consolidation
cards.body: When buyers and sellers are balanced, swings get smaller. Lines drawn through the highs and the lows converge and form a triangle.

cards.title: Three types
cards.body: Ascending: flat top, rising lows. Descending: flat bottom, falling highs. Symmetrical: both lines slope toward each other.

cards.title: The break matters most
cards.body: The direction of the break matters more than the name. Ascending triangles break up somewhat more often than down, but not reliably enough to trade the name alone.

cards.title: Late in the triangle
cards.body: If price drifts all the way to the tip without breaking, the pattern loses its meaning. A break with a candle close and volume is clearer than one that leaks out at the very end.

cards.prompt: Which pattern formed before the break?
cards.explain: A flat ceiling with rising lows is an ascending triangle. Here it broke upward.

cards.question: A flat top with rising lows forms…
cards.explain: Flat resistance, rising support: ascending.

cards.question: Shrinking swings inside a triangle usually mean…
options: Buyers and sellers are in balance
cards.explain: Balance first; the break shows who wins. Nothing is sure.

cards.question: What matters more than a triangle's name?
cards.explain: Trade the break, not the label.

cards.title: Where the stop goes
cards.body: After a breakout from a triangle, a logical stop sits back inside the triangle – often below the last swing low before the break.

cards.title: The flagpole
cards.body: A flag starts with a sharp, almost vertical move – the pole. Then price pauses in a small channel that drifts slightly against the move – the flag.

cards.title: Pennant
cards.body: A pennant is the same idea, but the pause forms a small symmetrical triangle instead of a channel.

cards.question: A flag is usually considered a…
cards.explain: A pause inside a strong move.

cards.title: What makes a good flag
cards.body: A strong pole, a short and shallow flag, and shrinking volume during the pause. A flag that drifts back most of the pole is no longer a flag.

cards.prompt: Tap the candle that broke out of the pause.
cards.explain: The break from the pause is where continuation traders act – with a stop back inside the pause.

cards.title: The usual estimate
cards.body: Traders sometimes project the pole's length from the breakout point. Like all measured moves, it's a rough guide.

cards.question: During a healthy flag, volume usually…
cards.explain: A quiet pause, then the next push.

cards.question: The 'flag' has drifted back 80% of the pole. It is…
cards.explain: Too deep – the momentum is gone.

cards.title: Rising wedge
cards.body: Both lines slope up, but they converge: highs rise more slowly than lows. Each push gains less – a sign of tiring buyers. It often breaks down.

cards.title: Falling wedge
cards.body: Both lines slope down and converge: each new low is only slightly lower. Sellers are losing strength. It often breaks up.

cards.question: Rising lines that converge, with smaller and smaller gains. This is…
cards.explain: Rising but tiring.

cards.title: Wedge vs. triangle
cards.body: In a triangle, at least one line is flat or the lines slope toward each other from opposite sides. In a wedge, both lines slope in the same direction.

cards.question: In a wedge, both lines…
cards.explain: Same direction, converging.

cards.title: 'Often' isn't 'always'
cards.body: Wedges are tendencies, not rules. Wait for the actual break and plan the stop on the other side of the wedge.

cards.prompt: Draw the rising support line under these lows.
cards.explain: In a rising wedge this lower line is the one watched for a break.

cards.question: A falling wedge usually signals…
cards.explain: Smaller new lows = less selling power.

cards.title: Why estimate a target?
cards.body: Before entering, traders want to know if there is enough room to make the risk worth it. A measured move gives a rough idea of that room.

cards.title: The common rule
cards.body: Measure the height of a pattern or range, and project it from the breakout point. Range 50–60 broken upward → rough target near 70.

cards.question: Range 40–48 breaks upward. A rough measured target is…
cards.explain: Height 8, projected from 48.

cards.title: Check what's in the way
cards.body: If a major resistance sits halfway to the target, the 'room' is really only to that resistance. Obstacles beat formulas.

cards.prompt: Drag the target so the trade is about 2:1 reward-to-risk.
cards.explain: Twice the distance to the stop. Compare it with the room the chart offers.

cards.title: Targets are not predictions
cards.body: Price may stop short or run far beyond. Many traders take partial profits near the estimate and let the rest follow a trailing stop.

cards.question: The measured target is 70, but strong resistance sits at 64. Realistic room is…
cards.explain: Obstacles first.

cards.question: A measured move is best described as…
cards.explain: A planning tool, not a forecast.

cards.title: Bigger timeframe, bigger level
cards.body: A support level visible on the weekly chart represents months of decisions by many traders. A level on a 5-minute chart may represent an hour.

cards.question: Which level usually matters more?
cards.explain: More time, more participants.

cards.title: Mark big levels first
cards.body: A useful routine: mark weekly and daily levels first, then switch to your trading timeframe. Small-timeframe setups that run into a big level often stall.

cards.title: Confluence
cards.body: When several things line up at one price – a daily support, a round number, a trend line – traders call it confluence. More reasons, more attention.

cards.question: A daily support, a round number and a trend line all meet at 100. This is…
cards.explain: Several reasons at one place.

cards.prompt: A wide range from a higher timeframe: drag the line onto its support.
cards.explain: Big swings, but the same floor kept holding.

cards.title: Don't overdo it
cards.body: Confluence improves odds; it doesn't create certainty. Five reasons at one level can still fail – the stop stays.

cards.question: A 5-minute breakout runs straight into weekly resistance. What's likely?
cards.explain: Big levels absorb small moves.

cards.title: Every idea has an 'I'm wrong' price
cards.body: Before entering, ask: at what price does this pattern stop making sense? That is the invalidation level, and it's where the stop belongs.

cards.title: Examples
cards.body: Breakout above resistance: wrong if price closes back inside the range. Double bottom: wrong below the lows. Uptrend: wrong below the last higher low.

cards.question: You traded a double bottom with lows at 40. Where is it invalidated?
cards.explain: Breaking the lows breaks the pattern.

cards.prompt: Tap the candle that broke above resistance before failing.
cards.explain: That close looked like a breakout. When price closed back in the range, the idea was invalidated.

cards.title: If the stop is too far
cards.body: Sometimes the logical invalidation is so far away that the risk is too big. The answer is a smaller position or no trade – not a closer, illogical stop.

cards.question: The logical stop is too far for your risk limit. You should…
cards.explain: Size adapts to the stop, not the other way around.

cards.title: Accept it quickly
cards.body: When the invalidation level breaks, the plan says exit. Hoping, waiting or 'giving it room' turns small losses into big ones.

cards.question: The invalidation level just broke. The disciplined move is…
cards.explain: The plan was made with a clear head.

cards.title: Step 1: structure
cards.body: On your main timeframe, label the last few swings. Uptrend, downtrend or range? Check the higher timeframe agrees.

cards.title: Step 2: levels
cards.body: Mark two or three key zones around the price: major highs and lows, round numbers, broken levels that may flip.

cards.question: What do you mark right after the structure?
cards.explain: A few clear zones.

cards.title: Step 3: the setup
cards.body: Is there a pattern at a level – a breakout, a retest, a double bottom, a flag? If not, the map is still useful: it tells you to wait.

cards.title: Step 4: wrong and right
cards.body: Write the invalidation price (stop) and the room to the next obstacle (target). If the room isn't at least about twice the risk, many traders pass.

cards.prompt: Final map check: drag the line onto the neckline.
cards.explain: The neckline was the level that decided this chart.

cards.question: Room to the next resistance is 3, risk to the stop is 3. Many traders would…
cards.explain: 1:1 leaves little margin for being wrong.

cards.question: No pattern at any level today. Your map says…
cards.explain: No setup is a decision too.

exam.question: Lower highs and lower lows describe…
Resistance is an area where…
A common breakout filter is to wait for…
options: A candle close beyond the level

exam.question: A head and shoulders usually appears after…
exam.explain: The inverse version follows a downtrend.

exam.question: A flat bottom with falling highs is…
LH and LL describe…
Broken resistance holding as support on a pullback is called…
A double top completes when price…
options: Closes below the low between the peaks
exam.explain: The middle low is the trigger.

exam.question: A flag is usually a…
exam.explain: A pause inside a strong move.

exam.question: The stop belongs at…
options: The price where the idea is wrong

cards.title: Math on top of price
cards.body: An indicator is a calculation made from price (and sometimes volume). It doesn't know anything the chart doesn't – it presents the same information in another way.

cards.title: Lagging by design
cards.body: Because indicators use past candles, they react after price moves. A moving average turns up only after price has already been rising for a while.

cards.question: Why do moving averages turn after price does?
cards.explain: Averages of the past move after the present.

cards.title: Two families
cards.body: Trend indicators (moving averages, MACD) describe direction. Oscillators (RSI, stochastic) swing between fixed values and describe momentum. Volume tools show participation.

cards.question: RSI belongs to which family?
cards.explain: It swings between 0 and 100.

cards.title: No magic settings
cards.body: Sellers of 'secret settings' are selling a story. The common default values work as well as any – what matters is how you use the tool and manage risk.

cards.prompt: Here MA 20 is drawn in yellow. Where does it mostly sit?
cards.explain: In a rising market the average of recent prices trails below the price.

cards.question: An indicator can tell you…
options: A summary of past price behavior
cards.explain: Description, not prediction.

cards.title: Smoothing the noise
cards.body: A moving average (MA) is the average closing price of the last N candles. A simple MA weighs every candle equally; an exponential MA (EMA) gives recent candles more weight.

cards.title: Reading the trend
cards.body: Price above a rising MA is the context of an uptrend; below a falling MA, a downtrend. Common lengths: 20 for the short term, 50 for the medium term, 200 for the long term.

cards.title: Crossovers
cards.body: When a short MA crosses above a long one, people call it a 'golden cross'; crossing below is a 'death cross'. They describe what already happened, not what will happen.

cards.title: The catch: lag
cards.body: MAs are built from past prices, so they always react late. In sideways markets they cross back and forth and give many false signals. Try MA 20 and MA 50 on the trading floor charts.

cards.prompt: Tap the candle where MA 20 (yellow) crossed above MA 50 (purple).
cards.explain: The cross came well after the low. Moving averages confirm a turn late; that's the lag.

cards.question: A 20-period moving average is…
options: The average of the last 20 closes
cards.explain: It averages the last 20 closes; it never predicts.

cards.question: The main weakness of MA crossovers is…
options: They lag and whipsaw in sideways markets
They predict the future too well
cards.explain: Built from the past, they react late and flip often in ranges.

cards.question: A 50-period moving average reacts to new prices…
cards.explain: Longer average = smoother and slower.

cards.title: Common lengths
cards.body: 20 for the short-term trend, 50 for the medium term, 200 for the long term. They're popular because so many people watch them – not because the numbers are special.

cards.title: Simple moving average
cards.body: The SMA gives every candle in the window the same weight. A 20-SMA is just the sum of the last 20 closes divided by 20.

cards.title: Exponential moving average
cards.body: The EMA gives more weight to recent candles, so it reacts faster to new moves – and also to noise.

cards.question: Which reacts faster to a sudden move?
cards.explain: More weight on recent prices.

cards.title: The trade-off
cards.body: Fast averages give earlier signals and more false ones. Slow averages give fewer false signals but later. There's no free lunch – only a choice.

cards.question: What do you give up by using a slower average?
cards.explain: Fewer false signals, but later ones.

cards.title: Pick one and stay consistent
cards.body: Switching between SMA and EMA to find the 'right' picture after the fact is a trap. Choose one for your method and judge results over many trades.

cards.prompt: Tap the candle where MA 20 (yellow) crossed above MA 50 (purple).
cards.explain: The faster line crossed the slower one well after the turn – the lag you just learned about.

cards.question: Trying many average types until one fits past trades is…
cards.explain: It fits the past, not the future.

lessons.title: Moving averages as a trend filter

cards.title: Above or below
cards.body: A simple filter: when price is above a rising 200-day average, the long-term trend is up; below a falling one, it's down. Many traders only look for longs in the first case.

cards.question: Price is below a falling 200-day MA. The long-term trend is…
cards.explain: Below a falling average = downtrend.

cards.title: Dynamic support
cards.body: In steady trends, pullbacks often pause near a popular average like the 20 or 50. It's a zone of interest, not a wall.

cards.title: The slope matters
cards.body: A flat moving average with price crossing it back and forth means no trend. In that case the average is mostly noise.

cards.question: Price keeps crossing a flat MA up and down. This suggests…
cards.explain: Flat average, no direction.

cards.prompt: Where is price compared with MA 20 (yellow) for most of this chart?
cards.explain: Price stayed below a falling average – the filter says 'downtrend'.

cards.title: A filter, not a trigger
cards.body: Use the average to decide which direction to look for, then use structure and levels for the actual entry and stop.

cards.question: How do many traders use the 200-day average?
cards.explain: Direction first, details later.

lessons.title: Golden cross, death cross and whipsaws

cards.title: The famous crosses
cards.body: A golden cross is the 50-day average crossing above the 200-day. A death cross is the opposite. Headlines love them.

cards.question: A golden cross is…
cards.explain: Fast average over slow average.

cards.title: Very late signals
cards.body: By the time a 50 crosses a 200, the move is usually well underway. The cross confirms what price showed weeks earlier.

cards.title: Whipsaws
cards.body: In sideways markets, averages cross back and forth, producing signal after signal that fails. Each costs a small loss plus fees.

cards.question: Crossover signals fail again and again. The market is probably…
cards.explain: Ranges create whipsaws.

cards.prompt: Tap the candle of the crossover (MA 20 over MA 50).
cards.explain: Compare the cross with the low of the move: most of the rise from the bottom came before the signal.

cards.title: Using crosses sensibly
cards.body: Crosses can describe the regime – trending or not – rather than trigger trades. Combined with structure, they help avoid fighting a big trend.

cards.question: A golden cross headline appears. The most accurate reading is…
options: A late confirmation of a rise
cards.explain: Lagging, not predictive.

cards.title: What RSI measures
cards.body: The Relative Strength Index compares average gains with average losses over the last 14 candles and shows the result from 0 to 100. It measures momentum: how strongly price has been moving.

cards.title: 70 and 30
cards.body: Above 70 is often called 'overbought', below 30 'oversold'. In a strong trend RSI can stay above 70 for weeks while price keeps rising, so these levels are context, not a timer.

cards.title: Divergence
cards.body: If price makes a higher high but RSI makes a lower high, momentum is fading: a bearish divergence. The mirror image is a bullish divergence. It is a warning sign, not an exact timing tool.

cards.title: Use it with context
cards.body: RSI works best together with the trend and key levels. Every instrument on the trading floor shows its RSI with a short explanation.

cards.prompt: Tap the first candle where RSI rose above 70.
cards.explain: RSI went above 70 as the breakout picked up speed. Notice price kept rising afterwards: 'overbought' isn't a sell signal.

cards.question: In a strong uptrend, RSI above 70…
options: Can stay there for a long time
cards.explain: Strong momentum keeps RSI high. 'Overbought' is not a sell signal by itself.

cards.question: Price makes a higher high, RSI a lower high. This is…
cards.explain: Rising price, falling momentum: a warning that the move is tiring.

cards.question: RSI is calculated from…
cards.explain: It compares the size of up moves and down moves.

cards.title: The default
cards.body: The common setting is 14 periods. 70 and 30 are the classic thresholds, but they're conventions, not laws.

cards.title: RSI shifts with the trend
cards.body: In strong uptrends RSI tends to stay between about 40 and 80; in downtrends between about 20 and 60. 'Overbought' readings are normal in a strong rise.

cards.question: In a strong uptrend RSI stays above 70 for days. This means…
options: Strong momentum, not automatically a top
cards.explain: Overbought can stay overbought.

cards.title: Where RSI 30/70 works better
cards.body: In ranges, RSI near 30 tends to line up with the range floor and near 70 with the ceiling. Context decides how to read the same number.

cards.prompt: Tap the first candle where RSI rose above 70.
cards.explain: RSI crossed 70 as momentum built – and price kept going for a while. Overbought isn't a sell signal by itself.

cards.title: The 50 line
cards.body: Some traders watch RSI crossing 50 as a simple momentum filter: above 50, gains have outweighed losses recently.

cards.question: In a sideways range, RSI near 30 often lines up with…
cards.explain: Oscillators fit ranges best.

cards.question: RSI is above 50. Recently…
cards.explain: 50 is the balance point.

cards.title: Read it with price
cards.body: RSI is most useful as a second opinion on what price structure already shows – not as a standalone buy or sell button.

cards.title: Bearish divergence
cards.body: Price makes a higher high, but RSI makes a lower high. The rise continued with less momentum behind it – a warning, not a reversal signal on its own.

cards.title: Bullish divergence
cards.body: Price makes a lower low, but RSI makes a higher low: selling momentum is fading even as price dips.

cards.question: Price: higher high. RSI: lower high. This is…
cards.explain: Momentum disagrees with price on the upside.

cards.title: Divergence can last
cards.body: Strong trends can show divergence several times before turning. Traders who sell on every divergence get run over.

cards.title: Wait for price to confirm
cards.body: A sensible approach: treat divergence as an alert, then wait for a structure break – like a lower low after the bearish divergence.

cards.question: You spot bearish divergence in a strong uptrend. A sensible step is…
options: Treat it as an alert and wait for structure
cards.explain: Alert first, confirmation second.

cards.prompt: RSI is shown below. During the breakout, did RSI confirm the move?
cards.explain: RSI rose with price and reached high values: momentum confirmed the move. No divergence here.

cards.question: Price: lower low. RSI: higher low. This hints…
cards.explain: Bullish divergence.

cards.title: Where's the close in the range?
cards.body: The stochastic measures where the latest close sits within the high–low range of the last N candles (often 14): 100 = at the top, 0 = at the bottom.

cards.question: Stochastic reads 95. The latest close is…
options: Near the top of the recent range
cards.explain: High reading = close near the range high.

cards.title: Two lines
cards.body: %K is the raw value; %D is a short average of it. Crosses of the two lines and moves above 80 or below 20 are the classic readings.

cards.title: Fast and jumpy
cards.body: The stochastic is more sensitive than RSI, so it gives many signals – and many false ones in trends. It suits ranges better.

cards.question: Compared with RSI, the stochastic is usually…
cards.explain: Speed costs reliability.

cards.title: Same family, same information
cards.body: RSI and stochastic both measure momentum from the same prices. Using both doesn't double your evidence – it repeats it.

cards.question: RSI and stochastic both say 'overbought'. How much new evidence is that?
options: Little – they measure the same thing
cards.explain: Two thermometers in the same room.

cards.prompt: In this range, where would an oscillator like the stochastic usually read high?
cards.explain: Near the ceiling, the close sits at the top of the recent range – high readings.

cards.title: Built from two averages
cards.body: The MACD line is a 12-period EMA minus a 26-period EMA. The signal line is a 9-period EMA of the MACD line. The histogram shows the gap between the two.

cards.title: Crossings
cards.body: MACD crossing above its signal line means short-term momentum is turning up; crossing below, turning down. A shrinking histogram shows momentum fading before the lines cross.

cards.title: The zero line
cards.body: Above zero, the short average is above the long one, which fits an uptrend. Below zero fits a downtrend. Crossings that agree with that side tend to be cleaner.

cards.title: Same caveat
cards.body: Because MACD is built from moving averages, it lags like them. Traders use it to confirm what price already shows, not to predict.

cards.question: The MACD line is the difference between…
cards.explain: 12 EMA − 26 EMA.

cards.question: A histogram shrinking toward zero suggests…
cards.explain: The gap between MACD and its signal is closing.

cards.question: The MACD line is built from…
options: The gap between two moving averages
cards.explain: Typically 12- and 26-period EMAs.

cards.title: Zero line
cards.body: MACD above zero means the fast average is above the slow one – upward momentum on that timeframe. Below zero, the opposite.

cards.title: The signal line
cards.body: The signal line is an average of the MACD line (often 9 periods). MACD crossing above it is the classic bullish trigger; crossing below, bearish.

cards.title: The histogram
cards.body: The bars show MACD minus the signal line. Growing bars mean momentum is accelerating; shrinking bars mean it's slowing, even if price still rises.

cards.question: Price still rises but the MACD histogram shrinks. This shows…
cards.explain: Smaller bars = less acceleration.

cards.title: Lag on lag
cards.body: The signal line averages an indicator that already averages prices. Its crosses are late, and in ranges they whipsaw like any crossover.

cards.question: MACD crosses below its signal line. The classic reading is…
cards.explain: Down-cross = momentum turning down.

cards.title: Divergence works here too
cards.body: Price making higher highs while MACD peaks get lower is the same warning you saw with RSI – and needs the same price confirmation.

cards.question: Why are MACD signal-line crosses late?
cards.explain: Double smoothing, double lag.

cards.prompt: MACD is based on moving averages. Tap where MA 20 crossed above MA 50.
cards.explain: When the fast average moves above the slow one, MACD (their gap) turns positive.

cards.title: Average True Range
cards.body: ATR measures how much price typically moves per candle, including gaps. An ATR of 2 on a daily chart means a typical day moves about 2 points.

cards.question: Stock A has an ATR of 1, stock B an ATR of 5. Which swings more per day?
cards.explain: Bigger ATR, bigger typical moves.

cards.title: No direction
cards.body: ATR says how much, not which way. A rising ATR can come with a rally or a crash.

cards.title: Stops that fit the market
cards.body: A stop tighter than one ATR is likely to be hit by normal noise. Many traders place stops beyond a level plus a fraction of ATR – more in module 6.

cards.question: ATR is 3. A stop 0.5 away from entry is…
options: Likely to be hit by normal noise
cards.explain: Much smaller than a typical candle.

cards.title: Size by volatility
cards.body: If one stock moves twice as much as another, the same number of shares carries twice the risk. ATR helps compare and size positions fairly.

cards.prompt: Buying near the top of the range: drag the stop to a logical place, beyond normal noise.
cards.explain: A little below support, with room for a typical candle's swing.

cards.question: ATR doubles. What should usually change?
cards.explain: Keep risk in money constant.

cards.title: Bands around an average
cards.body: Bollinger Bands are a 20-period MA with a band two standard deviations above and below. The bands widen when the market is volatile and narrow when it is quiet.

cards.title: The squeeze
cards.body: Very narrow bands mean volatility is low. Quiet periods are often followed by bigger moves, but the bands do not tell you the direction.

cards.title: A touch is not a signal
cards.body: In a strong uptrend price can 'walk' along the upper band for a long time. Touching a band says price is far from its average, nothing more.

cards.title: Volatility and stops
cards.body: When the bands are wide, normal swings are bigger, so a sensible stop is further away. With the same risk per trade, that means a smaller position.

cards.prompt: Tap the first candle that closed outside the bands after the squeeze.
cards.explain: The bands were narrow while the market was quiet, then the first close outside them came with the bigger move.

cards.question: The bands get very narrow. This tells you…
options: Volatility is low; a bigger move may follow
cards.explain: A squeeze describes volatility, not direction.

cards.question: Same risk per trade, but the bands are twice as wide. The position should be…
cards.explain: A wider stop with the same dollar risk means fewer units.

cards.question: Bollinger Bands are usually set at…
cards.explain: They widen and narrow with volatility.

cards.title: The squeeze
cards.body: When bands get unusually narrow, the market is unusually quiet. Quiet periods tend to be followed by bigger moves – but the squeeze doesn't tell you which way.

cards.prompt: Tap the first candle that closed outside the bands after the squeeze.
cards.explain: Quiet, quiet, then a close outside the band – the start of the expansion.

cards.question: A Bollinger squeeze tells you…
options: A bigger move may come, direction unknown
cards.explain: Volatility, not direction.

cards.title: Walking the band
cards.body: In strong trends, price can 'walk' along the upper band for many candles. Touching the band is not a reason to sell in that case.

cards.question: Price hugs the upper band for 10 candles in a row. This suggests…
cards.explain: Band walks happen in strong trends.

cards.title: Bands in ranges
cards.body: In a range, touches of the outer bands often line up with the range edges. Again: identify the regime first.

cards.question: Which question comes before reading the bands?
options: Is the market trending or ranging?
cards.explain: Regime first.

cards.title: Fake breaks from squeezes
cards.body: The first break out of a squeeze can be a head-fake that reverses. A stop on the other side of the squeeze limits that risk.

cards.title: How much traded
cards.body: Volume is how many shares or coins changed hands in a period. It is usually shown as bars under the price chart.

cards.title: Confirmation
cards.body: Moves with high volume show broad participation and tend to be more trustworthy. Breakouts on thin volume fail more often.

cards.title: Climax
cards.body: A huge spike in volume after a long move can mark exhaustion: everyone who wanted in got in. It is a clue to watch, not a certainty.

cards.title: Fewer is better
cards.body: Every indicator is calculated from the same price and volume. Ten indicators repeat the same information and create conflicting signals. One or two you truly understand beat a crowded chart.

cards.question: A breakout on very low volume is…
cards.explain: Thin participation makes failure more likely.

cards.question: Why do many traders use only one or two indicators?
options: They're all built from the same price data
cards.explain: More indicators repeat the same data and add confusion.

cards.question: A breakout on volume twice the average is…
cards.explain: More participation behind the move.

cards.title: Relative volume
cards.body: Compare volume with its own recent average, not with other stocks. 'High' means high for this market.

cards.title: Volume confirms trends
cards.body: In a healthy uptrend, volume tends to be higher on up days and lower on pullbacks. The opposite pattern is a warning.

cards.question: In an uptrend, volume is high on down days and low on up days. This is…
cards.explain: Sellers are more active than buyers.

cards.title: Climax volume
cards.body: An enormous volume spike after a long move can mark exhaustion: the last buyers (or sellers) rushing in at once.

cards.title: Drying up
cards.body: Volume that fades during a pullback or a pattern shows little interest in pushing the other way – often a quiet setup before the next move.

cards.question: Volume dries up during a pullback in an uptrend. This often means…
cards.explain: A quiet pullback is a healthy one.

cards.prompt: Tap the breakout candle – the one that usually carries extra volume.
cards.explain: Breakouts that come with a jump in participation are more convincing.

cards.title: Crypto volume caution
cards.body: Volume is spread across many exchanges, and some report inflated numbers. Prefer volume from large, reputable venues.

cards.question: A huge volume spike after a long rally may signal…
cards.explain: Everyone who wanted in got in.

cards.title: Volume-weighted average price
cards.body: VWAP is the average price of the day, weighted by how much traded at each price. It resets every session.

cards.question: VWAP gives more weight to prices where…
cards.explain: Volume-weighted.

cards.title: Who uses it
cards.body: Large funds often judge their execution against VWAP: buying below it counts as a good fill. That's why intraday traders watch it.

cards.title: Above or below
cards.body: Price above VWAP means buyers have paid up today; below means sellers have been in control. Many day traders favor longs above it.

cards.question: Price is well below VWAP most of the day. This suggests…
cards.explain: Below the day's average = weaker day.

cards.title: An intraday tool
cards.body: Because it resets daily, VWAP matters mostly for day trading. On daily or weekly charts it isn't the right tool.

cards.question: For a swing trader on daily charts, standard VWAP is…
options: Of limited use – it resets daily
cards.explain: Right tool, right timeframe.

cards.question: Why do many day traders watch VWAP?
cards.explain: Watched levels attract activity.

cards.title: The tool
cards.body: Fibonacci retracements draw levels at 23.6%, 38.2%, 50%, 61.8% and 78.6% of a move. Traders watch them for where a pullback might pause.

cards.question: A move from 100 to 200. The 50% retracement level is…
cards.explain: Halfway back: 200 − 50 = 150.

cards.title: Why it 'works' sometimes
cards.body: There is no proven natural law here. The levels get reactions partly because many traders watch them, and partly because with five levels, price is always near one.

cards.question: Why should you be skeptical of Fibonacci 'magic'?
options: With many levels, price is always near one
cards.explain: Many lines = easy to find a 'hit' afterwards.

cards.title: Use it with structure
cards.body: A Fibonacci level that lines up with an old support or a trend line (confluence) is more interesting than one in empty space.

cards.question: Which Fibonacci level deserves more attention?
options: One that lines up with prior support
cards.explain: Confluence beats a lone line.

cards.prompt: Tools aside, where did buyers actually defend? Drag the line onto support.
cards.explain: Price itself shows the defended zone. Tools like Fibonacci are only useful if they agree with it.

cards.title: Drawing it consistently
cards.body: Draw from a clear swing low to a clear swing high (or the reverse in a downtrend). Moving the anchors until a level 'fits' is just hindsight.

cards.title: More isn't better
cards.body: Five momentum indicators on one chart give the same message five times. They also create conflicting signals that freeze decisions.

cards.title: One from each family
cards.body: A clean setup: structure and levels from price, one trend tool (a moving average), one momentum tool (RSI), and volume. Each answers a different question.

cards.question: Which combination adds the most different information?
options: A moving average, RSI and volume
Three moving averages of similar length
cards.explain: Trend + momentum + participation.

cards.title: When they disagree
cards.body: Disagreement is information: maybe the trend is up but momentum is fading. The honest response is often a smaller position or no trade.

cards.question: Trend is up, momentum is fading, volume is weak. A sensible response is…
cards.explain: Mixed evidence, reduced risk.

cards.question: Your chart has 8 indicators and you can't decide. The fix is…
cards.explain: Clarity over clutter.

cards.prompt: MA 20 (yellow) and MA 50 (purple). What do they show at the end of this chart?
cards.explain: The fast average ended above the slow one: the trend tool says 'up'. Now you'd check momentum and volume separately.
options: Fast above slow – trend turned up

cards.title: Price has the final word
cards.body: If indicators say 'up' but price breaks its last higher low, price wins. Indicators describe price; they don't overrule it.

cards.title: Write the rule exactly
cards.body: 'RSI looks oversold' can't be tested. 'Buy when RSI(14) closes above 30 while price is above the 200-day MA; stop below the last low' can.

cards.question: Which rule can actually be tested?
options: 'Buy when RSI(14) closes above 30, stop below the last low'
cards.explain: Exact conditions, exact exits.

cards.title: Look at many examples
cards.body: Go back through the chart and record every case the rule triggered – including the ugly ones. Fifty examples tell you more than five.

cards.title: Beware hindsight
cards.body: It's easy to skip examples that 'obviously' wouldn't count. If the rule triggered, it counts. Otherwise you're testing your memory, not the rule.

cards.question: While testing, you skip triggers that 'didn't look right'. This leads to…
cards.explain: Cherry-picking flatters the method.

cards.title: Include costs
cards.body: Subtract spreads and fees from every trade in the test. Many 'profitable' ideas with lots of small trades disappear once costs are counted.

cards.question: A test shows small profits on 300 tiny trades, before costs. Next step?
options: Subtract costs – they may erase it
cards.explain: Costs scale with trade count.

cards.title: Then practice forward
cards.body: After a test on the past, practice the rule forward in the trading floor with virtual money. New data is the real exam.

exam.question: An EMA differs from a simple MA because it…
RSI ranges from…
A bullish divergence is when…
options: Price makes a lower low but RSI a higher low

exam.question: Bollinger Bands widen when…
Adding a tenth indicator to a chart usually…
Compared with an SMA, an EMA of the same length…
RSI above 70 in a strong uptrend…
ATR tells you…
VWAP resets…
A good indicator combination covers…

modules.title: Risk management & methods
modules.subtitle: The skill that keeps you in the game

cards.title: The only goal you control
cards.body: You can't control whether the next trade wins. You can control how much it costs if it loses. Professional traders think about the loss first.

cards.title: Stay in the game
cards.body: A trader with a decent method who risks small survives the bad streaks and lets the method work. A trader who risks big can be wiped out before the edge shows up.

cards.question: What can you actually control on each trade?
options: How much you lose if it fails
cards.explain: Risk is the controllable part.

cards.title: Remember the recovery math
cards.body: From module 1: −50% needs +100% to recover. Big losses aren't just painful; they're mathematically hard to undo.

cards.question: Two traders have the same method. A risks 1% per trade, B risks 15%. Over a bad streak…
options: B may be wiped out; A survives
cards.explain: Same edge, different survival.

cards.title: Defense wins careers
cards.body: Most of this module is about defense: stops, sizing, limits and your own psychology. Strategies come and go; risk control is what lasts.

cards.prompt: First, the defense: you buy near the top of this range. Drag the stop to a logical place.
cards.explain: Below support with a small buffer – the price where the idea is wrong.

cards.question: Which question comes first when planning a trade?
cards.explain: Loss first, profit second.

cards.title: Drawdown
cards.body: A drawdown is the drop from your account's peak to its lowest point afterwards. From $10,000 down to $8,500 is a 15% drawdown, even if you later recover.

cards.question: Account peaked at $20,000 and fell to $15,000. The drawdown is…

cards.title: Drawdowns are normal
cards.body: Every method has them. A realistic plan expects drawdowns of several times your risk per trade and doesn't panic or change everything mid-way.

cards.title: Risk of ruin
cards.body: Risk of ruin is the chance of losing so much that you can't continue. It grows very fast as risk per trade grows – far faster than most people feel.

cards.question: Doubling your risk per trade makes the chance of ruin…
cards.explain: Ruin risk rises steeply with size.

cards.title: A simple illustration
cards.body: Ten losses in a row at 1% each leave about 90% of the account. At 5% each, about 60%. At 10% each, about 35%. Streaks like that happen to every trader eventually.

cards.question: 10 losses in a row at 5% each leave about…

cards.title: Know your number
cards.body: Decide in advance the drawdown at which you stop, review and practice again before continuing – for example 10% for a beginner.

cards.title: Where the idea is wrong
cards.body: A stop belongs at the price that proves your trade idea wrong, for example a little below the support you bought at. A random '5% below' ignores what the chart is telling you.

cards.title: Give it room
cards.body: Stops that are too tight get hit by normal noise. ATR (Average True Range) measures how much price usually moves per candle; many traders keep the stop at least one ATR beyond the level.

cards.title: Gaps
cards.body: A stop becomes a market order when it is touched. If price gaps past it, the order fills at the next available price, which can be much worse. The trading floor simulates this.

cards.title: Never widen it
cards.body: Moving a stop further away to avoid a loss turns a small, planned loss into a big, unplanned one. Moving it in your favor to protect gains (a trailing stop) is a different decision.

cards.prompt: You buy near the top of this range. Drag the stop to a logical place.
cards.explain: A logical stop sits a little below support: if support breaks, the idea is wrong. Too close and noise hits it; too far and the loss gets big.

cards.question: You buy near support at 50. A logical stop is…
cards.explain: If support fails, the idea is wrong. That's where the stop goes.

cards.question: ATR measures…
options: How much price typically moves per candle
cards.explain: Average True Range = typical movement, used to size stops.

cards.question: Moving your stop further away because price is getting close is…
cards.explain: It turns a planned loss into an unplanned one.

cards.title: Stop first, size second
cards.body: Find the logical stop from the chart, then calculate the position size that fits your risk. Never pick the size first and squeeze the stop to fit.

cards.title: Structure stops
cards.body: Placed beyond a level that defines the idea – below support, below the last higher low. If that level breaks, the reason for the trade is gone.

cards.title: Volatility stops
cards.body: Placed a multiple of ATR away from entry, for example 1.5 × ATR. It adapts to how wild the market is, but ignores chart levels unless you combine them.

cards.question: ATR is 2. A 1.5 × ATR stop for a long at 50 sits at…

cards.title: Combining both
cards.body: A common approach: the structure level plus a small ATR buffer. Logical and fitted to current volatility.

cards.title: Time stops
cards.body: If a trade was supposed to move quickly and hasn't after a set time, some traders exit anyway. Capital stuck in a dead trade can't be used elsewhere.

cards.question: A breakout trade goes nowhere for two weeks. A time stop would…
options: Close it and free the capital
cards.explain: No movement = the idea isn't working.

cards.prompt: A structure stop with a buffer: drag it to a logical place below support.
cards.explain: Just under the floor, with room for a normal wick.

cards.question: What does a structure stop protect against?
options: The trade idea being proven wrong
cards.explain: It exits when the reason is gone.

cards.title: Trailing a stop
cards.body: As a trade moves in your favor, you can raise the stop behind it – under each new higher low, or a fixed ATR distance below price. It locks in part of the gain.

cards.question: In a long trade, a trailing stop moves…
cards.explain: It ratchets in your favor only.

cards.title: Too tight, too early
cards.body: Trailing too closely gets you stopped out by normal pullbacks, right before the trend continues. Give the trade room to breathe.

cards.title: Break-even stops
cards.body: Moving the stop to the entry price removes the loss – but also raises the chance of being shaken out. Many traders wait until price has moved about 1R first.

cards.question: Moving the stop to break-even right after entry usually…
options: Gets you stopped out by noise more often
cards.explain: No risk, but more shake-outs.

cards.prompt: Trailing under structure: tap two rising lows to draw the line a stop could follow.
cards.explain: As each higher low forms, a structure trailing stop moves up under it.

cards.title: Exits define results
cards.body: Entries get the attention, but how you exit winners decides whether the average win is big enough to pay for the losers.

cards.question: Where does a structure-based trailing stop go in an uptrend?
cards.explain: Each new HL is the new line in the sand.

cards.title: Measuring in R
cards.body: Risk is the distance from entry to stop. Reward is the distance from entry to target. If you risk 5 to make 10, the trade is 2:1, often written as 2R.

cards.title: The break-even win rate
cards.body: With 2:1 trades you break even, before costs, if a bit more than one trade in three wins. With 1:1 you need over half. The formula: 1 ÷ (1 + R).

cards.title: Realistic targets
cards.body: A target should come from the chart, such as the next resistance, not from a wish. A 5:1 target that price never reaches is worth less than a 2:1 that is reached often.

cards.title: Practise it
cards.body: The Chart Trainer's virtual trade and the order ticket on the trading floor both calculate R for you, so you can see it before every trade.

cards.prompt: Drag the target so the trade is about 2:1 reward-to-risk.
cards.explain: 2:1 means the distance to the target is twice the distance to the stop.

cards.question: Entry 100, stop 95, target 110. Reward-to-risk is…
cards.explain: Reward 10, risk 5 → 2:1.

cards.question: With 2:1 trades, the break-even win rate before costs is about…
Risk $2 per share, target $5 away. Reward-to-risk is…

cards.title: Three common ways
cards.body: A fixed target (for example 2R or the next resistance), a trailing stop that lets winners run, or a mix: take part at a target, trail the rest.

cards.question: Which method lets winners run the furthest?
cards.explain: No ceiling until the trend breaks.

cards.title: Partial exits
cards.body: Selling half at 1.5–2R and trailing the rest reduces the emotional pressure and still leaves room for a big move.

cards.title: The trade-off
cards.body: Fixed targets win more often but cap the winners. Trailing exits win less often but catch the occasional big run. Neither is free.

cards.question: You sell half at the target and trail the rest. The benefit is…
options: Locked-in gains plus a chance at a bigger move
cards.explain: A balance of both worlds.

cards.prompt: Set the first target: drag it to about 2:1 reward-to-risk.
cards.explain: Twice the stop distance – a common place to take part of the position.

cards.title: Don't cut winners from fear
cards.body: A common beginner pattern: take profits quickly but let losses run. That's the exact opposite of what the math needs.

cards.question: 'Small wins, big losses' usually comes from…
options: Exiting winners early and holding losers
cards.explain: Fear on winners, hope on losers.

cards.title: Two numbers, one result
cards.body: A method can win 70% of the time and lose money, or win 35% of the time and make money. What matters is win rate combined with the average win and loss.

cards.question: Win rate 35%, average win 3R, average loss 1R. Before costs this method…

cards.title: The high-win-rate trap
cards.body: Winning 90% of trades feels great – until one big loss erases fifty small wins. Methods with tiny targets and wide stops often look like this.

cards.question: Win 90% at +0.1R each, lose 10% at −2R each. Expectancy?

cards.title: Low win rates need patience
cards.body: Trend-following methods often win 30–40% of the time. Long losing streaks are normal and psychologically hard. Pick a style you can actually stick with.

cards.title: Costs shift everything
cards.body: Fees and spreads reduce every win and enlarge every loss. Methods with small R per trade suffer most.

cards.question: Which statement is true?
options: Win rate alone doesn't show profitability
Higher win rate is always better
cards.explain: You need both numbers.

cards.title: Measure, don't guess
cards.body: Your journal gives you the real numbers: win rate, average win, average loss. Many traders are surprised how different they are from what they felt.

cards.title: The real question
cards.body: The question is not how many shares you can afford, but how much you lose if the stop is hit. Position size turns that loss into a number you chose in advance.

cards.title: The formula
cards.body: Size = (account × risk %) ÷ (entry − stop). Example: $10,000 account, 1% risk = $100. Entry 50, stop 48: $100 ÷ $2 = 50 shares.

cards.title: Why a small percentage
cards.body: Ten losses in a row happen to everyone eventually. At 1% per trade you keep about 90% of the account; at 10% per trade you keep about 35%. That is why many traders stay around 1–2%.

cards.title: Leverage
cards.body: Leverage lets you control more than your money, and it multiplies losses exactly like gains. It does not change the math above; it only makes mistakes bigger and faster.

cards.question: $20,000 account, 1% risk, entry 50, stop 48. How many shares?
After 10 losses in a row risking 10% each, about how much is left?
cards.explain: 0.9¹⁰ ≈ 0.35. At 1% per trade it would be about 90%.

cards.question: $10,000 account, 1% risk, entry 25, stop 24. How many shares?
cards.explain: $100 risk ÷ $1 per share = 100.

cards.title: Round down
cards.body: If the formula says 137.6 shares, buy 137 – never round up. And if the position value is more than you have, the trade is too big for this stop: skip it.

cards.title: Same risk, different size
cards.body: A calm stock might need a 2% stop; a volatile coin might need 10%. With the same 1% account risk, the coin position must be five times smaller.

cards.question: $10,000 account, 1% risk ($100). Stop is 10% below entry. Position value?

cards.title: The formula again
cards.body: Position value = money at risk ÷ stop distance in %. Wider stops mean smaller positions – automatically.

cards.question: Same $100 risk, stop 2% away. Position value?

cards.title: Gaps and weekends
cards.body: Stocks can gap past stops overnight; crypto can crash on a weekend. For assets that jump, many traders size even smaller than the formula says.

cards.prompt: A volatile coin: drag the line onto its support. Notice how far it is from the top.
cards.explain: A stop below this support is far from the price – so the position must be small.

cards.title: Feel the money, not the units
cards.body: Owning '1 coin' or '100 shares' means nothing alone. Always translate a position into 'how much do I lose at the stop?'.

cards.question: Which question translates a position into risk?
options: How much do I lose if the stop is hit?
How many units do I own?
cards.explain: Risk is money at the stop.

cards.title: Hidden doubling
cards.body: Five trades risking 1% each in five tech stocks may behave like one 5% bet: on a bad day for tech, they all hit their stops together.

cards.question: Three positions in Bitcoin, Ethereum and Solana, 1% risk each. Effective risk is closer to…
cards.explain: Major coins tend to move together.

cards.title: Correlation
cards.body: Correlation measures how much two assets move together, from −1 (opposite) to +1 (identical). Assets in the same sector or theme are usually highly correlated.

cards.title: A total-risk cap
cards.body: Many traders cap total open risk – for example 3–5% of the account across all positions – and count correlated positions as one.

cards.question: Your total-risk cap is 4%. You have four open trades at 1% each. A fifth trade…
cards.explain: The cap is the cap.

cards.title: Freeing up risk
cards.body: When a trade's stop is moved to break-even, it no longer carries open risk. That's one way room appears for new trades.

cards.question: Correlation of +0.9 between two stocks means…
cards.explain: Close to +1 = similar moves.

cards.title: Diversify the risk, not just the names
cards.body: Different tickers aren't diversification if they share the same driver. Ask what single piece of news could hit all your positions at once.

cards.title: Circuit breakers for you
cards.body: Exchanges halt trading when prices crash. Traders can do the same for themselves: stop for the day after losing, say, 2–3% or three trades in a row.

cards.question: Why stop trading after a set daily loss?
options: Losses affect judgment; it prevents spirals
cards.explain: Protect yourself from yourself.

cards.title: Why it works
cards.body: After losses, people tend to take worse trades to 'make it back'. A hard limit stops a bad day from becoming a disastrous one.

cards.title: Weekly and monthly limits
cards.body: A weekly limit (for example 5%) or a drawdown limit (for example 10%) triggers a pause, a review of the journal, and practice before trading again.

cards.question: You hit your weekly loss limit on Wednesday. The plan says…
cards.explain: The limit only works if it's absolute.

cards.title: Write it before you need it
cards.body: Set limits when calm and write them in your plan. In the middle of a losing day, every limit feels negotiable.

cards.question: When is the best time to set a loss limit?
cards.explain: Decide with a clear head.

cards.title: Winning streaks too
cards.body: Some traders also slow down after a big winning day. Overconfidence after wins causes oversized, careless trades.

cards.title: Write it down
cards.body: For every trade, note the setup, entry, stop, target, size, result and how you felt. Patterns in your own decisions are invisible until you write them down.

cards.title: Expectancy
cards.body: Expectancy = win rate × average win − loss rate × average loss. It tells you what one trade is worth on average over many trades. A method needs a positive number after costs.

cards.title: An example
cards.body: 40% winners averaging $300 and 60% losers averaging $100: 0.4 × 300 − 0.6 × 100 = +$60 per trade. You can lose more often than you win and still come out ahead.

cards.title: Sample size
cards.body: Ten trades prove nothing; luck dominates small samples. Judge a method after dozens of trades. The trading floor keeps your history and win rate for this.

cards.question: 50% winners averaging $200, 50% losers averaging $100. Expectancy per trade?
The main purpose of a trading journal is…
options: Learning from patterns in your own decisions
cards.explain: You can only fix what you can see.

cards.question: Win 40% at +2R, lose 60% at −1R. Expectancy?

cards.title: Count costs in expectancy
cards.body: Measure each trade's result after fees and spread. A method at +0.1R before costs can easily be negative after them.

cards.title: Your brain isn't built for this
cards.body: Losing money triggers the same alarm as physical danger. Under stress, people act fast and badly. Rules exist so you don't have to think clearly in those moments.

cards.title: Fear
cards.body: Fear makes you skip good setups after losses, exit winners too early, and hesitate on planned stops.

cards.title: Greed and FOMO
cards.body: Greed makes you size up after wins and chase moves that already ran. FOMO – fear of missing out – makes you jump in late, without a plan.

cards.question: A stock already jumped 30% today and you buy so you don't miss more. This is…
