cards.explain: Chasing is FOMO in action.

cards.title: Revenge trading
cards.body: After a loss, the urge to 'win it back' immediately leads to bigger, worse trades. It's one of the fastest ways to destroy an account.

cards.question: You just lost and want to win it back with a bigger trade now. The best move is…
cards.explain: Break the loop first.

cards.title: Practical defenses
cards.body: Pre-set orders (stop and target placed with the entry), a loss limit, a short break after each loss, and a journal entry that names the emotion.

cards.question: Which defense removes in-the-moment decisions?
options: Placing stop and target with the entry
cards.explain: Decide once, calmly.

cards.title: Confirmation bias
cards.body: Once you hold a position, you notice the news that agrees and ignore what doesn't. Before entering, write the strongest argument against your trade.

cards.question: You only read posts that agree with your position. This is…
cards.explain: Seeking agreement, not truth.

cards.title: Recency bias
cards.body: The last few trades feel like the whole story. Three losses make a good method feel broken; three wins make a bad one feel brilliant.

cards.title: Loss aversion
cards.body: Losses hurt about twice as much as equal gains feel good. That's why people hold losers 'until they come back' and sell winners too soon.

cards.question: Holding a losing trade 'until it comes back' is often driven by…
cards.explain: Avoiding the pain of realizing a loss.

cards.title: Overconfidence
cards.body: A few wins can make anyone feel skilled. Skill shows over hundreds of trades, not a lucky week.

cards.question: After three losses you want to abandon a method with 200 tested trades. This may be…
cards.explain: Three trades don't outweigh two hundred.

cards.title: Name it to tame it
cards.body: Write the bias in your journal when you notice it. Seeing 'FOMO' or 'revenge' written ten times is a powerful lesson.

cards.title: Day trading
cards.body: Positions are opened and closed the same day. Many small trades, so costs, speed and focus matter a lot. It is demanding and most beginners find it the hardest style.

cards.title: Swing trading
cards.body: Trades last days to weeks and aim to catch one swing, for example from support toward resistance. Fewer decisions, but positions stay open overnight and over weekends.

cards.title: Trend following
cards.body: Positions are held as long as the trend lasts. Most trades are small losses or small wins; a few big trends pay for them. It needs patience and discipline.

cards.title: No style is best
cards.body: Pick by your time, temperament and costs, and write a plan: what you trade, when you enter, where you exit and how much you risk. Test it on the trading floor before anything else.

cards.question: Which style holds trades for days to weeks?
cards.explain: Swing trading aims to catch one swing over days or weeks.

cards.question: A trading plan should define…
options: Entry, exit and risk before the trade
cards.explain: Decisions made in advance are calmer than decisions made under pressure.

cards.question: Which style usually needs the most screen time?
cards.explain: Intraday decisions need constant attention.

cards.title: Fit your life
cards.body: If you work full-time, day trading may simply not fit. Swing or trend styles on daily charts can be studied and practiced in the evening.

cards.title: Before the session
cards.body: Check the economic calendar and earnings dates, update your chart maps, and write the few setups you're watching with their entries, stops and targets.

cards.question: What should you check before the session?
cards.explain: Know the landmines in advance.

cards.title: A short watchlist
cards.body: Five instruments you know well beat fifty you glance at. The trading floor's watchlist (star icon) is built for exactly this.

cards.title: During the session
cards.body: Act only on setups from your list. Place stop and target with the entry. Then step back – staring at every tick invites impulsive changes.

cards.question: An exciting stock not on your list is moving fast. Your routine says…
options: Skip it – not part of today's plan
cards.explain: Unplanned trades are FOMO trades.

cards.title: After the session
cards.body: Journal every trade, note whether you followed the plan, and once a week review the numbers. Improvement comes from the review, not the trading.

cards.question: Where does most improvement come from?
cards.explain: Reflection turns experience into skill.

cards.title: Keep it boring
cards.body: Good routines are repetitive. If trading feels like a casino, something in the process is missing.

cards.title: More trades, worse results
cards.body: Every trade pays costs, and boredom trades are rarely good setups. Many accounts are ruined not by one big loss but by hundreds of unnecessary small ones.

cards.question: You trade because the market is open and you're bored. This is…
cards.explain: No setup, no trade.

cards.title: Signs of overtrading
cards.body: Trading setups not in your plan, lowering your standards late in the day, many trades after a loss, and feeling restless without a position.

cards.title: A trade limit
cards.body: A maximum number of trades per day or week forces you to choose only the best setups. The free trading floor's 3 trades a day works the same way.

cards.question: What does a daily trade limit encourage?
cards.explain: Scarcity makes you selective.

cards.title: Doing nothing is a position
cards.body: Cash is a valid choice. Waiting for a clear setup is a skill, not a waste of time.

cards.prompt: Price is in the middle of this range, far from both edges. What does a disciplined plan say?
cards.explain: The middle of a range offers no clear stop or edge. Waiting is the trade.

cards.question: Costs are $5 per trade. 400 trades a year cost…
cards.explain: Frequency multiplies costs.

cards.title: The five parts
cards.body: A complete method defines: the market and timeframe, the setup, the entry trigger, the stop and sizing, and the exit. Missing any part means improvising.

cards.question: Which is NOT one of the five parts of a method?
cards.explain: Tips are noise, not structure.

cards.title: An example
cards.body: Daily charts, liquid stocks. Setup: uptrend pullback to a former resistance. Trigger: bullish engulfing at the level. Stop: below the pattern. Size: 1%. Exit: half at 2R, trail the rest under higher lows.

cards.title: Simple beats clever
cards.body: A method you can explain in three sentences is easier to follow under stress than one with twelve conditions.

cards.question: Why prefer a simple method?
cards.explain: Consistency is the hard part.

cards.title: Test, then practice forward
cards.body: Check the rules over many past examples with costs, then practice forward on the trading floor for at least a few dozen trades before judging it.

cards.question: How many forward practice trades before judging a method?
cards.explain: Small samples mislead.

cards.title: Change one thing at a time
cards.body: If results disappoint after a fair sample, change a single rule and test again. Changing everything at once teaches you nothing.

cards.title: Not a requirement
cards.body: You don't have to trade real money at all. Understanding markets is valuable on its own – for investing, for your pension, and for spotting scams.

cards.title: If you decide to
cards.body: Many educators suggest: a positive record over a meaningful number of practice trades, a written plan, money you can truly afford to lose, and a licensed broker.

cards.question: Which is the most important condition before trading real money?
options: Only money you can afford to lose
cards.explain: Everything else comes after this.

cards.title: Start smaller than you think
cards.body: Real money feels different from virtual money – emotions get louder. Many traders start with a fraction of their planned size and grow only with evidence.

cards.question: Why start real trading with a smaller size than in practice?
options: Emotions are stronger with real money
cards.explain: Let your psychology catch up.

cards.title: Keep the same rules
cards.body: Same plan, same risk per trade, same journal. If results in real trading are much worse than in practice, the difference is usually discipline, not the market.

cards.title: This app stays education
cards.body: Chartora teaches skills and lets you practice with simulated prices. It doesn't give personal advice or tell you what to buy – those decisions are yours.

cards.question: Real results are much worse than practice results. The usual cause is…
cards.explain: The plan didn't change – the trader did.

exam.question: A stop-loss belongs where…
options: The trade idea is proven wrong

exam.question: Risking $50 to make $150 is…
Position size is calculated from…
Positive expectancy means…
options: On average a trade adds value over many trades
exam.explain: An average, not a promise per trade.

exam.question: Which is part of a written trading plan?
options: How much you risk per trade

exam.question: $10,000 falling to $8,000 is a drawdown of…
In a long trade, a trailing stop moves…
Win 35% at +3R, lose 65% at −1R. Expectancy is…
Five correlated positions at 1% each behave like…
After a loss, the urge to win it back right away is called…

cards.title: Money without a middleman
cards.body: Bitcoin was launched in 2009 as a way to send value directly between people, without a bank in the middle, using a public record kept by thousands of computers.

cards.title: What 'decentralized' means
cards.body: No single company or government runs the network. Rules are enforced by software that participants agree to run. That brings resilience – and no customer service.

cards.question: In a decentralized network, who can reverse your mistaken transfer?
cards.explain: No central party, no undo.

cards.title: Why prices move so much
cards.body: Most coins have no profits or dividends to anchor their value. Prices are driven by adoption, expectations, liquidity and sentiment – which change fast.

cards.question: What usually anchors a coin's price?
cards.explain: Little fundamental anchor = big swings.

cards.title: Supporters and critics
cards.body: Supporters see censorship-resistant money and new financial tools. Critics point to volatility, scams, energy use and little real-world use. Both have real arguments.

cards.prompt: A coin's chart over a few weeks. How would you describe it?
cards.explain: Large swings inside a wide range – typical for crypto.

cards.question: A benefit of decentralization is…
options: No single party can shut it down
cards.explain: Resilience, with fewer protections.

cards.title: A shared ledger
cards.body: A blockchain is a ledger copied on thousands of computers. New transactions are grouped into blocks, and each block is linked to the one before it, forming a chain.

cards.title: Hard to change
cards.body: Changing an old block would mean redoing the work for every block after it and convincing most of the network. That is why the history is very hard to rewrite.

cards.title: What it doesn't guarantee
cards.body: A blockchain records transactions; it does not make a coin valuable or a project honest. Thousands of projects on blockchains have failed or turned out to be scams.

cards.title: No undo button
cards.body: Crypto transfers are usually final. Send to the wrong address or to a scammer, and there is normally no bank to reverse it.

cards.question: A blockchain is mainly…
options: A shared ledger copied on many computers
cards.explain: A shared, hard-to-change record of transactions.

cards.question: You sent crypto to a scammer. Usually…
cards.explain: Transfers are final; prevention is the only protection.

cards.question: Who keeps copies of a public blockchain?
cards.explain: Shared and replicated.

cards.title: Transparent, not anonymous
cards.body: On Bitcoin and most blockchains every transaction is public. Addresses aren't names, but analysts can often link them to people.

cards.title: Public and private keys
cards.body: A wallet holds a private key – a secret number that can sign transactions. From it comes a public address that others can send to, like an account number.

cards.question: Which can you safely share?
cards.explain: Addresses receive; keys control.

cards.title: Not your keys, not your coins
cards.body: Whoever controls the private key controls the coins. On an exchange, the exchange holds the keys – you hold a promise.

cards.title: Check every character
cards.body: Addresses are long and unforgiving. Malware can swap a copied address for the attacker's. Check the first and last characters every time, and send a small test first for large amounts.

cards.question: Before a large transfer, a good habit is…
options: Send a small test and check the address
cards.explain: Mistakes are usually permanent.

cards.title: Right network, right token
cards.body: The same coin can exist on several networks. Sending on the wrong network can lose the funds. Match the network on both sides before sending.

cards.question: You pasted an address and the last characters look different from what you copied. You…
cards.explain: Clipboard hijackers swap addresses.

cards.question: Your coins are on an exchange. Who holds the private keys?
cards.explain: Custody means trust.

cards.title: Bitcoin
cards.body: Bitcoin, launched in 2009, was the first cryptocurrency. Its supply is capped at 21 million coins, which is why some call it 'digital gold'. Its price has still swung wildly.

cards.title: Ethereum
cards.body: Ethereum is a platform for smart contracts: programs that run on the blockchain. Its coin, ether, pays the fee ('gas') for running them.

cards.title: Altcoins
cards.body: There are thousands of other coins. Most are small and thinly traded, and a large share of them have lost almost all their value over time.

cards.title: Stablecoins
cards.body: Stablecoins are tokens designed to track a currency like the US dollar. They are only as safe as the issuer and its reserves; some have broken their peg and collapsed.

cards.question: Bitcoin's maximum supply is…
cards.explain: The cap is built into its rules.

cards.question: Smart contracts are…
options: Programs that run on a blockchain
cards.explain: Ethereum popularized them; ether pays for running them.

cards.question: A stablecoin's safety depends on…
cards.explain: Some stablecoins have lost their peg.

cards.title: Proof of work and proof of stake
cards.body: Bitcoin is secured by mining (proof of work), which uses a lot of electricity. Ethereum switched in 2022 to proof of stake, where validators lock up coins instead.

cards.title: Custodial
cards.body: An exchange or app holds the keys for you. Easy to use and recoverable with a password reset – but you depend on the company staying honest and solvent.

cards.title: Hot wallets
cards.body: Self-custody apps on a phone or browser. You hold the keys, but the device is online – exposed to malware and phishing. Good for small, everyday amounts.

cards.question: A browser wallet you use for new apps is best for…
cards.explain: Online = exposed.

cards.title: Cold storage
cards.body: A hardware wallet keeps keys on a small offline device that signs transactions without exposing the key. Buy only from the manufacturer, never second-hand.

cards.question: Why never buy a hardware wallet second-hand?
cards.explain: A pre-set device can be a trap.

cards.title: The trade-off
cards.body: Custodial: convenience, counterparty risk. Self-custody: control, and full responsibility for backups. Many people split funds between the two.

cards.question: The main risk of self-custody is…
options: Losing your backup means losing the coins
cards.explain: You are the bank – and the backup.

cards.title: When exchanges fail
cards.body: Large exchanges have collapsed – FTX in 2022 is the best-known case – freezing customers' money. Licensing and proof of reserves help, but don't remove the risk.

cards.title: The master key
cards.body: A seed phrase – usually 12 or 24 words – can recreate all the keys in a wallet. Anyone who has it owns everything in it.

cards.question: Where should a seed phrase be stored?
options: Offline, on paper or metal, in a safe place
cards.explain: Never digital, never online.

cards.title: Never digital
cards.body: No screenshots, cloud notes, emails or photos. Malware and hacked accounts scan for seed phrases.

cards.title: Nobody legitimate asks
cards.body: No exchange, wallet company or support agent will ever ask for your seed phrase. Any 'verification' page asking for it is theft.

cards.question: A 'wallet sync' site asks you to enter your 24 words. This is…
cards.explain: Typing the phrase anywhere online hands it over.

cards.title: Plan for fire and family
cards.body: Think about loss and inheritance too: a copy in a second safe place, and instructions your family could follow. Coins with a lost phrase are gone forever.

cards.question: You lose the only copy of your seed phrase and the device breaks. The coins are…
cards.explain: No backup, no recovery.

cards.question: Who should know your seed phrase?
cards.explain: It's the master key.

cards.title: On an exchange
cards.body: When you buy on a crypto exchange, it usually holds the coins for you. Convenient, but if the exchange fails or is hacked, you can lose access, as many customers did when FTX collapsed in 2022.

cards.title: Your own wallet
cards.body: In a self-custody wallet you hold the keys yourself. A seed phrase of 12 to 24 words can restore the wallet on any device.

cards.title: The seed phrase rule
cards.body: Anyone with your seed phrase owns your coins. Never type it into a website, never photograph it, never share it. No real support agent will ever ask for it.

cards.title: Check the platform
cards.body: Before using a crypto platform, check whether it is registered or licensed where you live. A slick app and big ads are not a license.

cards.question: 'Support' asks for your seed phrase to fix a problem. You…
options: Never share it: it's a scam
cards.explain: Real support never needs it. Whoever has it owns your coins.

cards.question: Keeping coins on an exchange means…
options: The exchange holds them and you depend on it
cards.explain: Custody means trusting the platform.

cards.question: What reduces exchange risk somewhat?
options: A licensed exchange and keeping only what you trade there
cards.explain: Limit what's exposed.

cards.title: Proof of reserves
cards.body: Some exchanges publish proof that they hold customers' coins. It helps, but it's a snapshot: it may not show debts, and it's only as good as the auditor.

cards.title: Network fees
cards.body: Every on-chain transfer pays a fee to the network (on Ethereum it's called gas). When many people transact at once, fees rise.

cards.question: Network fees usually rise when…
cards.explain: Demand for block space sets the price.

cards.title: Confirmations
cards.body: A transfer is final once it's included in a block and a few more blocks are added on top. Exchanges wait for a set number of confirmations before crediting you.

cards.title: Exchange fees too
cards.body: Exchanges charge trading fees, spreads and withdrawal fees. 'Zero commission' apps often earn through wider spreads.

cards.question: A 'zero commission' crypto app often earns through…
cards.explain: The cost is hidden in the price.

cards.title: Small amounts, big fees
cards.body: A $10 fee on a $50 transfer is 20%. For small amounts, fees can matter more than price moves.

cards.question: A $5 network fee on a $25 transfer is…

cards.title: No 'cancel' button
cards.body: Once confirmed, a transaction can't be called back. Unexpected fee-refund or 'stuck transaction' helpers who contact you are usually scammers.

cards.title: A fixed supply
cards.body: Bitcoin's rules cap the supply at 21 million coins. New coins are issued to miners as a reward for adding blocks, at a falling rate.

cards.title: The halving
cards.body: About every four years (every 210,000 blocks), the reward to miners is cut in half. The last halving was in April 2024; the next is expected around 2028.

cards.question: A Bitcoin halving cuts…
cards.explain: Less new supply, not a price rule.

cards.title: Halving and price
cards.body: Past halvings were followed by big rallies, but with only a handful of examples and many other factors, it's not a reliable law – and markets know the dates in advance.

cards.question: Why is 'halving = rally' an unreliable rule?
options: Few examples, many other factors, known in advance
cards.explain: Small samples mislead (module 2).

cards.title: Bitcoin ETFs
cards.body: Since 2024, spot Bitcoin ETFs trade on US exchanges, letting people get price exposure through a regular broker without holding keys. The price risk stays the same.

cards.question: Bitcoin's maximum supply is…
cards.explain: Set in the protocol.

cards.question: A Bitcoin ETF removes which risk?
cards.explain: Custody is handled; the price still swings.

cards.title: Programmable money
cards.body: Ethereum runs smart contracts: programs on the blockchain that move funds by fixed rules. Anyone can create a token on it in minutes.

cards.question: Creating a new token on Ethereum is…
options: Easy and cheap – anyone can do it
cards.explain: Which is why most new tokens are worthless.

cards.title: DeFi
cards.body: Decentralized finance apps let people trade, lend and borrow through smart contracts instead of banks. No account opening – and no deposit insurance.

cards.title: Code risk
cards.body: A bug in a smart contract can be exploited to drain all the funds in it. Hacks of DeFi apps have cost users billions over the years.

cards.question: The main extra risk of DeFi compared with a bank is…
cards.explain: Code is law – including its bugs.

cards.title: Approvals
cards.body: Using DeFi means approving contracts to move your tokens. Old, unlimited approvals stay active; review and revoke the ones you don't need.

cards.question: Why review old token approvals?
options: They can still be used to move your tokens
cards.explain: Unlimited approvals are open doors.

cards.question: Ethereum's smart contracts are…
options: Programs that run on the blockchain
cards.explain: Code that moves value by rules.

cards.title: Bigger moves
cards.body: Crypto moves much more than large stocks. Daily moves of 5–10% are common, and Bitcoin has fallen more than 70% from its peak several times.

cards.title: Smaller coins, wilder
cards.body: The smaller the coin, the larger the swings and the higher the chance it loses almost everything. Thin trading also means bigger spreads.

cards.title: What it means for risk
cards.body: Higher volatility means a wider stop, so for the same risk per trade the position must be smaller. Leverage on crypto has wiped out many accounts in minutes.

cards.title: Open all the time
cards.body: Crypto trades 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. Big moves can happen while you sleep. Compare Orbit Coin and Neox with a fund on the trading floor.

cards.prompt: A volatile coin: drag the line onto its support zone.
cards.explain: Same idea as in stocks, but the swings are much bigger, so stops need more room and positions must be smaller.

cards.question: Same 1% account risk, but the coin needs a stop twice as far as a stock. The position should be…
cards.explain: Twice the distance, same dollars at risk → half the units.

cards.question: Crypto markets are open…
cards.explain: No closing bell: plan for moves while you're away.

cards.question: Bitcoin falling 50% or more from a peak has happened…
cards.explain: Deep drawdowns are part of crypto's record.

cards.title: Backed by reserves
cards.body: Most large stablecoins aim to hold $1 by keeping reserves – cash and short-term government debt – for every coin issued. Their safety depends on those reserves really existing.

cards.title: Algorithmic stablecoins
cards.body: Some tried to hold $1 with code and a sister token instead of reserves. TerraUSD collapsed in May 2022, wiping out tens of billions of dollars in days.

cards.question: What mainly backs a reserve-based stablecoin?
cards.explain: Reserves are the anchor.

cards.title: Depegs
cards.body: When trust breaks, a stablecoin can trade below $1. Even reserve-backed coins have briefly depegged during banking scares.

cards.question: A stablecoin trades at $0.93. This is called…
cards.explain: It lost its $1 peg.

cards.title: Not a bank deposit
cards.body: Stablecoins aren't covered by deposit insurance. Regulation is growing – the EU's MiCA rules now apply to issuers there – but protections differ by country.

cards.question: What happened to TerraUSD in 2022?
cards.explain: An algorithmic peg failed under pressure.

cards.question: A stablecoin's safety depends on…
cards.explain: Check what really backs it.

cards.title: Thousands of coins
cards.body: There are many thousands of tokens. Most have tiny markets, and many lose almost all their value. A low price per coin says nothing about whether it's cheap.

cards.title: Market cap and FDV
cards.body: Market cap = price × coins in circulation. Fully diluted value (FDV) = price × all coins that will ever exist. A big gap means many new coins are coming.

cards.question: Price $1, 100M coins circulating, 1B coins in total. FDV is…
cards.explain: All coins × price.

cards.title: Unlocks
cards.body: Team and investor tokens are often locked and released on a schedule. Big unlocks can add selling pressure as early holders take profits.

cards.question: A large token unlock is coming next week. A likely effect is…
cards.explain: More supply hitting the market.

cards.title: Who holds it?
cards.body: If a few wallets hold most of the supply, they can move the price at will. Concentration is a risk worth checking.

cards.question: A coin costs $0.001. That means it's…
options: Nothing by itself – check market cap
cards.explain: Unit price ≠ value.

cards.prompt: Small coins swing hard. Drag the line onto this coin's support.
cards.explain: Even with wild swings, a defended floor shows where buyers stepped in – and where a stop would sit far below the price.

cards.title: Bitcoin leads
cards.body: Most coins tend to move with Bitcoin, often more sharply. When Bitcoin falls hard, it's rare for altcoins to hold up.

cards.question: Bitcoin drops 15% in a day. Altcoins usually…
cards.explain: High correlation, higher beta.

cards.title: Bitcoin dominance
cards.body: Dominance is Bitcoin's share of the total crypto market cap. Traders watch it to see whether money is flowing into Bitcoin or out to riskier coins.

cards.title: Weekends and nights
cards.body: Crypto trades 24/7, but liquidity is thinner on weekends and holidays. Sharp moves and wicks are more common when fewer traders are active.

cards.question: Why can weekend crypto moves be extra sharp?
cards.explain: Fewer orders in the book.

cards.title: Links to the wider market
cards.body: In recent years crypto has often moved with tech stocks and interest-rate expectations. It's not as separate from the rest of finance as early supporters hoped.

cards.question: Bitcoin dominance rising while altcoins fall suggests…
options: Money moving to the relatively 'safer' coin
cards.explain: Risk-off inside crypto.

cards.title: Your levels still work
cards.body: Structure, support and resistance, and risk management apply to crypto too – with wider stops and smaller positions.

cards.title: Rug pulls
cards.body: Developers hype a new token, attract buyers, then pull out the money backing it and vanish. The token's price collapses to almost nothing in minutes.

cards.title: Phishing and fake apps
cards.body: Lookalike websites, fake wallet apps and 'free airdrop' links ask you to connect your wallet and approve a transaction. That approval can let them drain it.

cards.title: Giveaways and fake friends
cards.body: 'Send 1 coin, get 2 back' is always a scam. So is an online 'friend' or romance who guides you to a platform showing huge fake profits, then demands fees to withdraw.

cards.title: Protect yourself
cards.body: Bookmark official sites, never share your seed phrase, treat guaranteed returns as a red flag, and report scams to the police and to the Israel Securities Authority.

cards.question: A new token's developers suddenly pull out the money and disappear. This is…
cards.explain: Classic rug pull: the buyers are left holding a worthless token.

cards.question: 'Send 1 coin and we'll send back 2' is…
cards.explain: Always a scam, even if it uses a famous name.

cards.question: A token's liquidity is 'locked' only by the developer's word. The risk is…
cards.explain: Promises aren't locks.

cards.title: Too new, too fast
cards.body: A token launched days ago, with anonymous developers and a price up 50× – the more of these boxes it ticks, the more likely it ends in a rug pull.

cards.title: Perpetual futures
cards.body: Many crypto exchanges offer 'perps': leveraged contracts that never expire, often with up to 100× leverage. Much of crypto's daily volume is in these contracts.

cards.question: With 50× leverage, roughly what move against you wipes out the margin?
cards.explain: 100% ÷ 50 = 2% (fees make it even less).

cards.title: Liquidation
cards.body: If losses reach your margin, the exchange closes the position automatically – a liquidation. In crypto's swings, a 2% move can take seconds.

cards.title: Liquidation cascades
cards.body: When many leveraged positions get liquidated at once, the forced selling pushes price further and triggers more liquidations. That's why crypto sometimes drops 10% in minutes.

cards.question: A sudden 10% crash in minutes, then a partial bounce, is often caused by…
cards.explain: Forced selling feeding itself.

cards.title: Funding rates
cards.body: Perps use a funding payment between longs and shorts to keep the price near spot. Holding leveraged positions for long can cost a lot in funding.

cards.question: For a beginner, high-leverage perps are…
options: One of the fastest ways to lose money
cards.explain: Module 1's rule: learn without leverage.

cards.title: Regulation varies
cards.body: Many regulators restrict high-leverage crypto products for retail clients. Offshore exchanges that offer 100× often provide little protection.

cards.title: Staking
cards.body: On proof-of-stake networks, holders can lock coins to help secure the network and receive rewards. The rewards come in the same volatile coin.

cards.question: You earn 5% staking rewards, but the coin falls 40%. Overall you…
cards.explain: Yield doesn't protect from price.

cards.title: Where does the yield come from?
cards.body: Always ask. Real sources: network rewards, borrowers paying interest, trading fees. If nobody can explain it, the yield may be paid from new deposits – a Ponzi.

cards.question: A platform offers 40% APY on a stablecoin and can't say where it comes from. This is…
cards.explain: Unexplained high yield = danger.

cards.title: Lending platforms failed
cards.body: In 2022 several crypto lending platforms that paid high yields froze withdrawals and went bankrupt. Depositors became creditors in long legal processes.

cards.title: Lock-up periods
cards.body: Some staking locks your coins for days or weeks. You can't sell during a crash. Know the unlock rules before committing.

cards.question: Your coins are locked for 21 days and the market crashes. You…
cards.explain: Liquidity has a price.

cards.title: APY vs. APR
cards.body: APY includes compounding; APR doesn't. Platforms often show the bigger-looking number. Neither is guaranteed.

cards.title: Memecoins
cards.body: Memecoins are tokens built around a joke, an animal or a trend, usually with no purpose beyond trading. Prices are pure attention and sentiment.

cards.question: What usually drives a memecoin's price?
cards.explain: No cash flows, all sentiment.

cards.title: The lottery-ticket math
cards.body: You hear about the few that went up 1,000×. Thousands of others went to zero. Survivorship bias (module 3) is at its strongest here.

cards.question: Stories of 1,000× memecoin gains show…
cards.explain: The zeros don't make headlines.

cards.title: Insiders and snipers
cards.body: Launch insiders and bots often buy in the first seconds and sell to later buyers. Many new memecoins are designed as pump-and-dumps from day one.

cards.title: NFTs
cards.body: NFTs are unique tokens linked to images, art or items. Prices swung from extreme highs in 2021 to deep lows later, and many collections can barely be sold today.

cards.question: The biggest practical risk with an obscure NFT or memecoin is often…
options: No buyers when you want to sell
cards.explain: Illiquidity traps you.

cards.title: If you play, size it like a ticket
cards.body: Treat any such purchase as money that may vanish completely, sized accordingly. It isn't investing, and it isn't a plan.

cards.title: Regulation is catching up
cards.body: Countries are building crypto rules. The EU's MiCA framework now licenses crypto service providers there; the US and Israel regulate parts of the market through existing and new laws.

cards.title: Use licensed services
cards.body: A licensed exchange must follow rules on client money, identity checks and disclosures. It doesn't remove price risk, but it removes some fraud risk.

cards.question: What does a license mostly protect you from?
options: Some fraud and misuse of client money
cards.explain: Rules for the firm, not for the market.

cards.title: Taxes apply
cards.body: In Israel, the Tax Authority treats crypto as an asset, so gains are generally subject to capital gains tax. Trades between coins can be taxable events. Rules change – ask a tax advisor.

cards.question: In Israel, swapping one coin for another may be…
cards.explain: Crypto is treated as an asset.

cards.title: Keep records
cards.body: Save every purchase, sale, swap and transfer with dates and amounts. Reconstructing years of crypto history later is painful and expensive.

cards.question: Why keep records of every crypto transaction?
cards.explain: Records save money and headaches.

cards.title: Not legal advice
cards.body: This lesson is general education. For your own situation, talk to a licensed tax advisor or accountant.

cards.title: Custody
cards.body: Decide what stays on a licensed exchange and what goes to self-custody. Keep large amounts offline and only small amounts in hot wallets.

cards.title: Keys and phrases
cards.body: Seed phrase on paper or metal, never digital, never shared. 2FA with an authenticator app on every account.

cards.question: Which setup is safest for a large long-term holding?
options: Hardware wallet with an offline seed backup
A hot wallet on your phone
An unknown exchange with high yield
cards.explain: Offline keys, offline backup.

cards.title: Transfers
cards.body: Check address and network, send a test first, and never trust 'support' who contacts you first.

cards.title: Risk
cards.body: Smaller positions than stocks, wider stops, no high leverage, and a clear answer to 'where does this yield come from?'.

cards.question: Compared with a calm stock, a crypto position with the same account risk should be…
cards.explain: Wider stop, smaller size.

cards.prompt: Last practice: drag the line onto this coin's support.
cards.explain: Same tools as stocks – just with more room and less size.

cards.question: A message offers help with your 'stuck' wallet if you share your phrase. You…
cards.explain: Never share any part of it.

exam.question: Why is a blockchain's history hard to rewrite?
options: Changes need redoing later blocks and most of the network

exam.question: Some call Bitcoin 'digital gold' because…
A stablecoin is designed to…
options: Track a currency like the dollar

exam.question: A seed phrase should be…
exam.explain: Whoever has it owns the coins.

exam.question: A token hyped by anonymous developers with locked selling is a sign of…
options: A likely rug pull or scam
exam.explain: If you can't sell, you can't exit.

exam.question: Which can you safely share?
A Bitcoin halving cuts…
exam.explain: Less new supply, not a price rule.

exam.question: A stablecoin trading at $0.90 has…

High yield nobody can explain is…

options: You own part of the company

placement.question: What is the bid–ask spread?
options: The gap between buy and sell prices

placement.question: An ETF that tracks an index…

options: Buyers pushed price back up after a drop

placement.question: Someone promises a guaranteed 20% a month. This is most likely…
'Act now, only 2 spots left!' is a sign of…

options: The average of the last 20 closes
A forecast of the next 20 days

placement.question: In a strong uptrend, RSI above 70…
options: Can stay there for a long time

A fall of about 20% or more from a peak.
The highest price a buyer currently pays.
The first cryptocurrency (2009), capped at 21 million coins.
A shared ledger of linked blocks kept by many computers.
A moving average with bands two standard deviations above and below.
A loan to a government or company that pays interest.
A close beyond a support/resistance level or pattern line.
Expecting or showing rising / falling prices.
The part of a candle between open and close.
Price and an indicator such as RSI move in different directions.
Spreading money across many assets to reduce single-asset risk.
Part of a company's profit paid out to shareholders.
A candle whose open and close are almost equal – indecision.
Exponential moving average: gives recent prices more weight.
A candle whose body fully covers the previous body.
Earnings per share – profit divided by the number of shares.
A fund traded like a stock, usually tracking an index.
Average result per trade: win rate × average win − loss rate × average loss.
A breakout that quickly returns inside the range.
When a candle opens far from the previous close, skipping prices.
Small body and long lower wick after a drop – a hint the drop is weakening.
Three peaks with the middle one highest; completes on a neckline break.
A measure that tracks a basket of stocks, e.g. S&P 500, TA-35.
Initial Public Offering – a company's first sale of shares to the public.
Controlling more than your own money; multiplies gains and losses.
An order that only fills at your price or better.
How easily an asset can be traded without moving its price.
A momentum indicator built from two moving averages.
A broker's demand for more money when losses eat your margin.
Share price × number of shares – the market value of a company.
An order to buy or sell immediately at the best available price.
The average closing price over the last N candles.
The line through the lows between the peaks of a head and shoulders.
Open, High, Low, Close – the four prices of a candle.
The list of waiting buy and sell limit orders at each price.
A fraud that pays old investors with new investors' money.
How many units you trade; set so a stop-out costs a small % of your balance.
Hyping a small asset, then selling to the late buyers.
Distance to target divided by distance to stop.
Relative Strength Index, 0–100; above 70 is often called 'overbought'.
Developers hype a token, then remove its money and disappear.
12–24 words that restore a wallet. Whoever has them owns the coins.
Selling borrowed shares to buy them back later, profiting if the price falls.
The difference between the expected price and the actual fill.
A program that runs on a blockchain, e.g. on Ethereum.
The gap between bid and ask – a hidden trading cost.
A token designed to track a currency such as the US dollar.
An order that exits a losing trade automatically at a set level.
Price areas where buying (support) or selling (resistance) tended to appear.
Holding trades for days to weeks to catch one price swing.
The period each candle covers: 1 minute, 1 hour, 1 day…
A record of every trade, its reasons and its result.
The direction of the market: higher highs and lows (up), lower highs and lows (down), or sideways.
A line through rising lows or falling highs.
Converging lines through highs and lows: ascending, descending or symmetrical.
How many units traded in a period.
Software or a device that holds the keys to your coins.
The thin line above or below the body, reaching the high or low.

stock.title: What a share is
stock.body: A unit of ownership in a company.

exchange.title: Exchange
exchange.body: A regulated marketplace reached through a licensed broker.

supplyDemand.title: Supply and demand
supplyDemand.body: More eager buyers push price up; more eager sellers push it down.

bidAsk.title: Bid vs. ask
bidAsk.body: Bid = best buyer's price. Ask = best seller's price.

spread.title: Spread
spread.body: Ask minus bid – a hidden cost.

limitOrder.title: Limit order
limitOrder.body: Your price or better – may not fill.

stopOrder.title: Stop order
stopOrder.body: Becomes a market order at a level; used to cut losses.

etf.title: ETF
etf.body: A fund traded like a stock, usually copying an index.

traderInvestor.title: Trader vs. investor
traderInvestor.body: Weeks vs. years; price vs. business.

riskOfLoss.title: Risk of loss
riskOfLoss.body: Only risk money you can afford to lose.

wick.title: Wick
wick.body: Reaches the period's high or low.

timeframe.title: Timeframe
timeframe.body: Longer timeframes usually give more meaningful patterns.

hammer.title: Hammer
hammer.body: Small body, lower wick ≥ 2× body, after a drop.

shootingStar.title: Shooting Star
shootingStar.body: Small body, long upper wick, after a rise.

engulfing.title: Engulfing
engulfing.body: Body fully covers the previous body.

signalGroups.title: 'Signal' groups
signalGroups.body: Urgency + screenshots + no license = marketing, not advice.

pumpDump.title: Pump & Dump
pumpDump.body: Late buyers become the organizers' exit.

guaranteedReturns.title: Guaranteed returns
guaranteedReturns.body: A guarantee of high returns = red flag.

checkLicense.title: Check a license
checkLicense.body: Use the regulator's register, not the firm's site.

trend.title: Trend
trend.body: Higher highs and lows = up; lower highs and lows = down.

trendline.title: Trend line
trendline.body: Connects rising lows (up) or falling highs (down); 2 points, ideally 3.

supportResistance.title: Support / resistance
supportResistance.body: Zones where falls or rises stopped before.

roleReversal.title: Role reversal
roleReversal.body: Broken resistance often becomes support, and vice versa.

breakout.title: Breakout
breakout.body: A close beyond a level, ideally with rising volume.

falseBreakout.title: False breakout
falseBreakout.body: Breaks out, then closes back inside the range.

headShoulders.title: Head and shoulders
headShoulders.body: Three peaks, middle highest; complete on a neckline break.

neckline.title: Neckline target
neckline.body: Head-to-neckline height projected from the break: an estimate.

triangle.title: Triangles
triangle.body: Ascending, descending, symmetrical; the break direction matters most.

consolidation.title: Consolidation
consolidation.body: Shrinking swings: buyers and sellers in balance.

movingAverage.title: Moving average
movingAverage.body: Average of the last N closes; EMA weighs recent ones more.

maCross.title: MA crossovers
maCross.body: Describe the past; lag and whipsaw in ranges.

divergence.title: Divergence
divergence.body: Price and momentum disagree: a warning, not timing.

macd.title: MACD
macd.body: 12 EMA − 26 EMA, with a 9 EMA signal line; lags.

bollinger.title: Bollinger Bands
bollinger.body: MA ± 2 standard deviations; a squeeze = low volatility.

volatility.title: Volatility and size
volatility.body: Wider normal swings → wider stop → smaller position.

volume.title: Volume
volume.body: Confirms moves; thin-volume breakouts fail more.

fewIndicators.title: Fewer indicators
fewIndicators.body: They all come from the same price data.

stopPlacement.title: Stop placement
stopPlacement.body: Where the idea is wrong; never widen it.

atrStop.title: ATR
atrStop.body: Typical movement per candle; keeps stops out of noise.

expectancy.title: Expectancy
expectancy.body: Win% × avg win − loss% × avg loss.

journal.title: Trading journal
journal.body: Record every trade; judge after dozens, not ten.

tradingStyles.title: Trading styles
tradingStyles.body: Day, swing, trend following: pick by time and temperament.

tradingPlan.title: Trading plan
tradingPlan.body: Entry, exit and risk decided before the trade.

blockchain.title: Blockchain
blockchain.body: A shared ledger of linked blocks, hard to rewrite.

irreversible.title: Final transfers
irreversible.body: Crypto transfers usually can't be undone.

bitcoin.title: Bitcoin
bitcoin.body: First crypto (2009), capped at 21 million coins.

stablecoin.title: Stablecoin
stablecoin.body: Tracks a currency; only as safe as its issuer.

exchangeRisk.title: Custody risk
exchangeRisk.body: Coins on an exchange depend on the exchange.

seedPhrase.title: Seed phrase
seedPhrase.body: Whoever has it owns the coins. Never share it.

cryptoVolatility.title: Crypto volatility
cryptoVolatility.body: Bigger moves → wider stops → smaller positions.

allDayMarket.title: 24/7 market
allDayMarket.body: No closing bell; moves happen while you sleep.

rugPull.title: Rug pull
rugPull.body: Developers pull the money and vanish.

cryptoPhishing.title: Crypto phishing
cryptoPhishing.body: Fake sites, airdrops and giveaways drain wallets.

shareholderRights.title: Shareholders are paid last
shareholderRights.body: In a bankruptcy, lenders come first; a stock can go to zero.

ticker.title: Ticker
ticker.body: A stock's short trading code, e.g. AAPL.

ipo.title: IPO
ipo.body: The first sale of shares to the public; the company gets the money.

primarySecondary.title: Primary vs. secondary market
primarySecondary.body: Primary: the company sells. Secondary: investors trade with each other.

broker.title: Choosing a broker
broker.body: Licensed by a real regulator, client money kept separate.

marketHours.title: Market hours
marketHours.body: Outside regular hours: fewer traders, wider spreads, bigger jumps.

orderBook.title: Order book
orderBook.body: The waiting bids and asks, with price and size.

liquidity.title: Liquidity
liquidity.body: How easily you can trade without moving the price.

volumeBasics.title: Volume
volumeBasics.body: Shares traded in a period; moves on high volume are more convincing.

slippage.title: Slippage
slippage.body: Expected price vs. actual fill – usually against you.

gapRisk.title: Gap risk
gapRisk.body: A gap can fill your stop far beyond its level.

stopLimit.title: Stop-limit
stopLimit.body: Triggers a limit order: no bad fill, but maybe no fill.

timeInForce.title: Day vs. GTC
timeInForce.body: Day orders expire; GTC orders stay until filled or cancelled.

longShort.title: Long vs. short
longShort.body: Long profits from a rise; short profits from a fall.

shortSelling.title: Short selling risk
shortSelling.body: Borrow, sell, buy back – the loss has no ceiling.

marketCap.title: Market cap
marketCap.body: Price × shares = company size. A low price isn't 'cheap'.

sectors.title: Sectors
sectors.body: Same sector, same news, similar moves.

diversify.title: Limits of diversification
diversify.body: It reduces single-company risk, not market risk.

bonds.title: Bonds
bonds.body: A loan to a state or company; prices fall when rates rise.

assetClasses.title: Risk and return
assetClasses.body: Higher possible return comes with bigger possible losses.

dividend.title: Dividend
dividend.body: Profit paid to shareholders; the price drops by about the payout.

earnings.title: Earnings reports
earnings.body: Quarterly results; stocks often gap after them.

expectations.title: Expectations
expectations.body: Prices react to the surprise, not the number.

interestRates.title: Interest rates
interestRates.body: Rising rates often pressure stocks, especially growth companies.

inflation.title: Inflation
inflation.body: Rising prices; central banks answer with higher rates.

volatilityBasics.title: Volatility
volatilityBasics.body: Bigger swings = wider stops, smaller positions.

fees.title: Trading costs
fees.body: Commission, spread, conversion, custody – judge results net.

capitalGainsTax.title: Tax on gains
capitalGainsTax.body: Profits are taxed (in Israel generally 25% on real gains).

compounding.title: Compounding
compounding.body: Returns on returns; exposes impossible promises.

leverage.title: Leverage
leverage.body: Magnifies gains and losses; 10× and −10% = wiped out.

marginCall.title: Margin call
marginCall.body: Add money or the broker closes your position.

planBasics.title: Trading plan
planBasics.body: What, why, stop, size, target – decided before entry.

journalBasics.title: Trading journal
journalBasics.body: Record every trade to find your patterns.

paperTrading.title: Process over outcome
paperTrading.body: Judge whether you followed the plan, not one result.

candleStory.title: Reading a candle
candleStory.body: Wicks are rejected prices; body size shows conviction.

closeLocation.title: Close location
closeLocation.body: Close near the high = buyers ended in control.

multiTimeframe.title: Top-down reading
multiTimeframe.body: Trend on the higher timeframe, timing on the lower.

marubozu.title: Marubozu
marubozu.body: All body, no wicks: one side controlled the whole period.

spinningTop.title: Spinning top
spinningTop.body: Small body, wicks both sides: momentum slowing.

rejectionWick.title: Rejection wick
rejectionWick.body: A wick ≥ 2× the body rejects that price area.

patternContext.title: Pattern context
patternContext.body: Trend + location + volume decide what a shape means.

hangingMan.title: Hanging Man
hangingMan.body: Hammer shape after a rise – a warning.

invertedHammer.title: Inverted Hammer
invertedHammer.body: Long upper wick after a drop – a weak bottom hint.

dojiTypes.title: Dragonfly vs. gravestone
dojiTypes.body: Dragonfly: long lower wick. Gravestone: long upper wick.

bearishEngulfing.title: Bearish engulfing
bearishEngulfing.body: After a rise, a red body covers the green one.

harami.title: Harami
harami.body: Small body inside the previous big body: the move paused.

insideBar.title: Inside bar
insideBar.body: Whole range inside the previous range: contraction.

piercingLine.title: Piercing line
piercingLine.body: Green closes above the middle of the previous red body.

darkCloud.title: Dark cloud cover
darkCloud.body: Red closes below the middle of the previous green body.

tweezer.title: Tweezers
tweezer.body: Matching lows (bottom) or highs (top) – a level rejected twice.

morningStar.title: Morning star
morningStar.body: Big red, small pause, big green – after a drop.

eveningStar.title: Evening star
eveningStar.body: Big green, small pause, big red – after a rise.

threeSoldiers.title: Soldiers and crows
threeSoldiers.body: Three strong candles in a row: steady pressure – or exhaustion late in a move.

candleGaps.title: Gaps
candleGaps.body: Open far from the previous close; not every gap fills.

momentumCandle.title: Momentum and climax
momentumCandle.body: Huge candles start moves – or end them.

confirmation.title: Confirmation
confirmation.body: Fewer failures in exchange for a worse entry.

candleStop.title: Pattern stops
candleStop.body: Just beyond the pattern's extreme, plus a buffer.

patternFailure.title: Pattern failure
patternFailure.body: Good setups still fail often; a failed signal is information.

sampleSize.title: Sample size
sampleSize.body: Judge a setup over dozens of trades, not a few.

candleChecklist.title: Candle checklist
candleChecklist.body: Trend → location → pattern → confirmation and risk.

licenseRule.title: Advice needs a license
licenseRule.body: Personal investment advice requires a license.

exitLiquidity.title: Exit liquidity
exitLiquidity.body: Hype creates buyers for insiders who are selling.

lifestyleMarketing.title: Lifestyle marketing
lifestyleMarketing.body: Luxury photos prove nothing; often the real income is courses.

ponzi.title: Ponzi scheme
ponzi.body: Old investors paid with new money; too-smooth returns.

pyramid.title: Pyramid scheme
pyramid.body: Income from recruiting, not from a real product.

fakeSocialProof.title: Fake social proof
fakeSocialProof.body: Followers, comments and celebrity videos can be faked.

fakeTrackRecord.title: Real track records
fakeTrackRecord.body: All trades, years, independently verified – not screenshots.

survivorship.title: Survivorship bias
survivorship.body: You see the lucky winners, not the silent losers.

cloneFirm.title: Clone firms
cloneFirm.body: Contact firms only via the regulator's register details.

impersonation.title: Bank impersonation
impersonation.body: No bank asks you to move money to a 'safe account'.

romanceScam.title: Romance scams
romanceScam.body: Online friend + investment platform = scam pattern.

phishing.title: Phishing
phishing.body: Never log in through a link you were sent.

twoFactor.title: 2FA codes
twoFactor.body: Use an authenticator app; never share a code.

remoteAccess.title: Remote access
remoteAccess.body: Never install screen-sharing for a caller.

walletDrainer.title: Wallet drainers
walletDrainer.body: Don't sign approvals you don't understand.

tradingBots.title: Bot promises
tradingBots.body: Daily % promises are impossible; backtests can be overfit.

managedAccount.title: 'We trade for you'
managedAccount.body: Never share logins; check license and custody.

pressureTactics.title: Pressure tactics
pressureTactics.body: Urgency, authority, sunk cost – answer with a 24-hour pause.

insiderTips.title: Insider tips
insiderTips.body: Real ones are illegal to use; fake ones are scams.

manipulation.title: Manipulation
manipulation.body: Spoofing fakes demand; wash trading fakes volume.

scamResponse.title: If you were scammed
scamResponse.body: Stop paying, call the bank, document, report.

scamChecklist.title: Scam checklist
scamChecklist.body: Who, what promise, what pressure, who holds the money, wait 24h.

marketStructure.title: Market structure
marketStructure.body: HH + HL = uptrend; LH + LL = downtrend.

swingPoints.title: Swing points
swingPoints.body: Local peaks and dips – the chart's skeleton.

pullback.title: Pullbacks
pullback.body: Trends move in waves; pullbacks build the higher lows.

trendStrength.title: Trend strength
trendStrength.body: Smaller pushes and deeper pullbacks = a tiring trend.

channel.title: Channels
channel.body: A trend line plus a parallel line; treat both as zones.

drawingZones.title: Drawing zones
drawingZones.body: Cover wicks and bodies; keep only the clearest levels.

roundNumbers.title: Round numbers
roundNumbers.body: Orders cluster at round prices; avoid crowded stops.

priorHighLow.title: Prior highs and lows
priorHighLow.body: Yesterday's and last week's extremes are widely watched.

rangeMarket.title: Ranges
rangeMarket.body: Edges matter, the middle doesn't; trend tools fail here.

retest.title: Break and retest
retest.body: Broken resistance tested as support; clearer stop, may miss the move.

structureBreak.title: How trends end
structureBreak.body: Lower high = warning; break of last higher low = end.

doubleTop.title: Double top / bottom
doubleTop.body: Completes on a close beyond the middle point.

flag.title: Flags and pennants
flag.body: Sharp pole, short shallow pause, shrinking volume.

wedge.title: Wedges
wedge.body: Both lines slope the same way and converge.

measuredMove.title: Measured moves
measuredMove.body: Pattern height projected from the break – check obstacles.

htfLevels.title: Higher-timeframe levels
